BasePK: 3866955

Speech:
Madam Speaker, the policies of this government have been undertaken because we do care about Canadians.
We are concerned about the future of Canada. We are concerned about the children of the present and the future. The problems we are facing in this country today and the reasons for some of these lay-offs that have had to take place are due to the fact that we have some very difficult fiscal problems in this country.

May 17, 1991
Supply
Some of these fiscal problems were started years ago when other governments attempted to fight recessions by spending, spending, spending. They were not spending those days' dollars. They were spending today's dollars, tomorrow's dollars, our children's and our grandchildren's dollars.
The Government of Ontario, run by a party which is the same as the party this member belongs to, is doing the very same thing in Ontario today that did not work for Canada in 1981-82, will not work for Ontario today and it is adding to the problems of this country.
I have children and I want to see them have a future. I want the Canadians of today to have jobs. That is why we are making the difficult economic decisions that have to be made to make us competitive in a global marketplace. We cannot build a wall around Canada and live by supplying the Canadian market only.
We can survive only by being competitive in a global market. Being competitive means working smarter and addressing problems, not by throwing money at them. That is the easy way out.
Any government can throw money it does not have by continuing to borrow on the future to try to solve a problem. Throwing money at problems does not solve them. Working at problems is what solves the problems of this country. Working together, management, labour, government and education. We cannot be competitive in this country if we do not have well-trained young people.
We cannot have our young people dropping out of school because they do not have a challenge, because they are not taught properly and because they are not given proper advice by the counsellors in the schools. We cannot be driving all our children into university educations.
We have to look at the trades. I attended a Skills Canada training competition last weekend in my riding, which brought together 200 students from across this country. They were building framings for housing. They were repairing motors. They were working on tin plates to fix furnaces and piping. They were working on electronic boards.
They were competing in a skills competition which proves that we have well skilled young people in this country who want to get involved in the jobs of the future
that are high-skilled. They are going to Louisville, Kentucky to compete. Canadians went last year and there was only one state in the U.S. that got more medals than Canada did at that competition.
They did it because we have young people who are interested in the skills and trades and who want to have jobs in the future. You cannot have jobs in the future of this country if you throw away the money today.
That is why we are taking very hard economic decisions. They are not easy. We do not like to sit here, make decisions and then read in the paper the next day that
1,000	jobs have been lost.
You do not have a monopoly on compassion in the NDP or in the socialist party of this country. There is as much compassion on this side of the House as there is on that side of the House.
We sat here and read statements about the Minister for International Trade from people who were saying: "Yes, there are problems with free trade in some industries but it is also helping industries."
The opposition members say: "That's bull." It is bull when they do not believe in it. When they get up and make false statements, they think they are speaking the truth. One does not hear those comments from this side of the House, at least not from the members who are here today.
We have no monopoly on behaviour in this House. If there were a little more decorum in this House, Canadians might start to believe a little more that we do things in this House.
That decorum comes from all sides of the House. It is something that all members should pay very special attention to. All members from all parties have a responsibility in this House to show the young people in this country that decisions that are made in this House are very important. That is why, as the Prime Minister said, this is the constituent assembly of Canada, this is where the decisions are going to be made, and this is where they are made with a great deal of heart, consideration and understanding, regardless of what the opposition says.
We are talking about governments in general. When the people of Canada don't believe in governments it is not only the government in power that they don't believe

in, it is all politicians, because of the behaviour of all politicians. We all have a role to play.

You are a research assistant analysing speeches from the Canadian House of Commons, 1953-1993.

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.
2. `procedural_score`: a number from 0 to 1 indicating how far the speech moves away from substantive policy discussion toward procedural, partisan, dilatory, or purely formal parliamentary language.

Topic rules:
- Be specific: "old-age pensions" not "social policy"; "railway freight rates" not "transportation".
- Lower-case unless a proper noun requires capitalisation.
- Ignore routine openings such as "Mr. Speaker".
- If substantive content is present, label the substantive topic.
- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

Score rule:
- 0 = almost entirely substantive policy, administration, legislation, public spending, economic/social issues, or government action.
- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.
- 1 = almost entirely procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal, with little substantive policy content.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.

Return only this JSON shape:
{"topic": "<short noun phrase>", "procedural_score": 0.0}

Speech:
Earlier in the day, as I had written the rotation, the representative of the Liberal Party would normally have been recognized. We did look as to what the rotation had been previously and realized

Supply
that I had made a mistake and we then advised the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan that a representative of his party would be next. The hon. members from the Liberal Party were advised that I had made a mistake and everything seemed to be normal.
I think that we should use the time for hon. members to make their representations and not for long points of order again.
I will recognize the hon. member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan.

BasePK: 3867015

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments on the hon. member for St. Boniface's response to the Speech from the Throne.
He made some very strong innuendoes, in fact, accusations that the federal government is practising its restraint on the backs of the provinces and the municipalities.
I think the figures really speak for themselves. Over the last six years, government restraint has controlled our expenditures at 3.7 per cent per year. The provincial governments' growth in their expenditures has averaged 6 per cent and 7 per cent and in some provinces, as high as 10 per cent. There was absolutely no impact on the transfer to the provinces up until this year's budget and last year's budget.
Last year, he implied we had a massive attack and although there was an increase, it was cut back by a half of 1 per cent over what it was planned. This is far, far less than a massive attack on provinces and municipalities.
I would ask the member for St. Boniface if he feels that the provinces should continue to spend way in excess of inflation, way in excess of what the federal government spends and should they not have any sense of restraint in their own programs?

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, Saturday evening in the Montreal Congress Centre the national Quebec tourism award ceremony was held.
I am very proud, Mr. Speaker, to report to this House today that Abitibi-Temiscamingue won top honours at that occasion, as the International Film Festival of Abitibi-Temiscamingue was awarded the most prestigious award, that is the Prix de ['excellence touristique (award of excellence in tourism), for contributing over the past ten years to the Quebec cultural and tourism recognition. This high distinction crowns ten years of efforts and relentless work to turn a regional festival into a national and even international event.
So, I want to congratulate, in my name and on behalf of my constituents, all the organizers of this festival for this great success. Well done!

May 21, 1991

BasePK: 3867096

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, that is certainly not the report we had on that Thursday meeting. The Minister of the Environment of Quebec has stated unequivocally that the problem he is having with his own cabinet arises out of a lack of support from this government for the environment. That is very clear and this minister is not going to get away with that kind of insipid, weak-kneed response.
The minister either takes a stand now or he stands forever condemned, along with his predecessors.
The issue is very, very clear. The Federal Court of Appeal has spoken. It said that the 1975 James Bay Agreement has the force of law. It has the force of federal law. This government has the right to move.
The only question in this House is: Why will this minister not stand up in this House and state unequivocally that this government will stand behind its own laws?

BasePK: 3867106

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. When I called the minister's 1-800 line regarding the Meme implant, it was still using figures saying the risk of cancer to women with Meme implants is equivalent to smoking one and a half cigarettes in a woman's lifetime and refers to only one in a million women facing cancer from the Meme. The FDA in the U.S. is saying one in 10,000, but some scientists from the FDA are stating one in 50, or one in 100.
Will the minister tell Canadian women who to believe and what is the minister planning to initiate to clarify for Canadian women the wide-ranging disparities coming from scientists?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, first of all, in response to my first question as minister of health and welfare, I would like to say that my primaiy interest is the health of Canadians, particularly women in this case. I think all

May 21, 1991
Oral Questions
our work, as minister responsible for the department, is for the health of Canadians.
In this case I believe that everything has been done to be as up-front as we could in terms of the information provided. The 1-800 line has been used over 500 times since it has been put in place a couple of weeks ago.
In the medical world, decisions are made in light of information that is available, and I believe that in terms of breast implants that is the basis on which our decision has been made. In this case all information available is referred to the department and, when necessary, we duplicate the control to be sure that the information is the best and we will continue to do that.
In light of the information that we have, a decision will be made in light of the health of all Canadians.

BasePK: 3867110

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister for International Trade, whomever he or she may be today.
A long time family-owned sawmill business in the upper Ottawa Valley which under normal conditions employed about 300 people has closed down its operations, taking 12 million badly needed dollars out of several small communities.
When is the government going to wake up? When is it going to get rid of the 15 per cent export tax? When is it going to lower the high Canadian dollar and give the forest industry and the forest workers a chance to survive? Where is the government's level playing field?

Mr. Speaker, this government is the eroding resource.
My supplementary is to the same minister. This government inflicted devastating measures on the forest industry and has done nothing concrete to date to change its destructive policies. This closure brings to approximately 3,000 the number jobs lost in the upper Ottawa Valley alone due to this government's policies.
When is the government going to get together with the big spenders at Queen's Park in Toronto and bring in a federal-provincial forestry agreement that will give the employers and the workers some hope for the future?

What is the government going to do for these unemployed people? Is there any mercy out there at all?

BasePK: 3867132

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, notice of which was initiated by my colleague, the member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, and which I confirmed as I was returning to the Chamber at about the time he was concluding his representation on my behalf. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for reserving for me that question of privilege.
Section 80, paragraph (2) of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fifth edition states in part:
A question of privilege-is a question partly of fact and partly of law-the law of contempt of Parliament-and is a matter for the House to determine.
I will show that the minister for immigration made an incorrect and misleading statement, which is therefore a question partly of fact.
Section 16 of Beauchesne also says:
Parliamentary privilege is the sum of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and by Members of each House individually, without which they could not discharge their functions -
I would like to underscore the phrase "and by Members of each House individually". Section 18 states:
-it is clear that many acts which might offend against the law or the moral sense of the community do not involve a Member's capacity to serve the people who have chosen him as their representative nor are they contrary to the usage nor derogatory to the dignity of the House of Commons.
I feel that it is contrary to the usage and derogatory to the dignity of this place when a member knowingly makes a statement that is incorrect. When such a false statement is used to assail the reputation of another hon. member the indignity to this House becomes more serious.

May 21, 1991
Privilege
Hence, when the hon. minister of immigration, in reply to my supplementary question during the proceedings of May 16, said, referring to me:
He was not even able to give me the name, the date of birth, or
address of the person we want.
This statement is on page 194 of Hansard. The minister, by his statement, impaired my ability to fully discharge my duties and obligations as a member of Parliament for Winnipeg North.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to submit the following as you consider my question of privilege:
First, with respect to the matter of the applicant's name, on May 9 I wrote a letter to the said hon. minister in which I indicated very clearly the name of the applicant visitor, Mrs. Surjit Kaur, for whom I have been making the representation. I am now prepared to table this letter if necessary. I should further inform the House that my office faxed a copy of this letter to the minister's office on the same date and the original was marked urgent and sent by messenger.
I should also inform the House that on May 13, in this Chamber, I personally approached the minister for follow-up and, once again, provided him with the name of the applicant. I am confident no member of Parliament would ever intercede for any person without knowledge of that person's name.
Second, with respect to the date of birth of the applicant visitor, my office was indeed unable to provide this information when first asked by the minister's staff, as we did not have it in our record at that time. However, on May 13 I furnished the minister's staff the date of birth, which is December 4, 1941.
I should add that the bereaved brother in Winnipeg approached the local immigration office on April 30, the day after the death of his brother, Mr. Sidhu Singh. One would assume all necessary information with respect to the applicant visitor, including the date of birth, should have been requested from the family at that time. I personally advised the minister's staff to kindly get in touch with the Winnipeg immigration office for further information.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to give my response to the Speech from the Throne.
The throne speech addressed three major concerns of Canadians: unity, prosperity and government responsiveness. All are intertwined.
The fragility of unity becomes apparent when our economy falters. It has also become apparent as our national debt has grown, compound interest on compound interest. We as a government must address these economic matters. We must also address the constitutional matters, and we are.
Today I would like to speak about Canadian unity from a different perspective. It is a narrow perspective, but it is one of utmost importance. I would like to discuss the importance of Canadian symbols.
I agree with all the debaters before me who have talked about the health of the economy and the structure of the Constitution and division of powers. Those are of paramount importance. However, we as Canadians have symbols. We must look back at what has united us as a country and at our common historical reality.
We have many, many symbols in this country. We have the flag, we have our institutions, we have common celebrations like Expo '67 and the Centennial celebrations of 1967. We will have one in 1992. We have common rituals, such as the singing of the anthem and the citizenship ceremony. All of these create a feeling of patriotism. We should increase and expand our use of symbols so we can quietly be proud of what we have achieved as a nation and as Canadians. These are positive things we can do to unite our country and our people.
All too often we forget about the benefits we have enjoyed as Canadians and our accomplishments as Canadians. I have been fortunate enough to do a little travelling. When I am in other countries, I realize how good we have it in Canada and for how much we have to be thankful.
We look inward as Canadians, when often we should be looking outward. We have made contributions to peace and freedom through two World Wars, the Boer War, the Korean War and the recent war. Our achievements continue. These are the achievements of Roy Brown and Billy Bishop.
Next year, Canada will celebrate its 125th birthday. In 1927, Canada celebrated its 60th birthday. At that time, celebrations were held and Canadians rejoiced about Canada and the contributions they made to the world.
The Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII, toured Canada to celebrate our Diamond Jubilee. That year, the Confederation Building, which is part of the House of Commons, was opened. It was to commemorate Canada's 50th birthday. During Canada's 50th birthday we were involved in a war and celebrations were postponed for 10 years.
Canada should commemorate our 125th birthday by opening our Parliament Buildings to Canadians. The Parliament Buildings are one of the most important symbols we have as Canadians. They have become crowded, overused and overworked.
There are plans to reallocate space and build a visitor reception centre in the basement in the entrance under the Peace Tower, where there could be a theatre, public washrooms and some displays. We should do this without hesitation or trepidation. A small expenditure like this is money which is not wasted.
The Government of Canada should help Canadians to recognize their achievements by building symbols like statues and monuments. I am not that dumb. I am at least prepared to listen to what they have to say. I am at least prepared to hear their arguments. If someone would figure out a way that we can elect a Senate, fine. If someone can figure out what they are going to do after we elect them, I think that is pretty important. If someone can suggest some changes in the relationship between the Senate of Canada and the House of Commons that would work, I am prepared to hear that argument and to accept it. Everybody else in this Chamber had better be prepared to hear it and accept it as well.
Governments at all levels in this country are being challenged and not in polite academic ways. They are being challenged on the streets, in the factories, in the playgrounds, in the arenas every day all across Canada,
and it seems that governments cannot hear it. That is a tragedy.
I have followed for some time the government's frustration with the Question Period. I have seen it here and in the other Chamber. I am amazed that somehow anybody in his or her right mind feels that if we limit it to 30 seconds, that will solve the problem. That is not the problem.
I have heard really good questions in other chambers go on much longer than 30 seconds. If people know what they are talking about, are reasonably secure in their facts and are putting forward good arguments, it is not a question of whether it is 29 seconds long or four minutes long. It is a question of relevance.
As I listen to my constituents talk about this Chamber, that is the question they have on their minds: "What the hell is going on down there?" I have to admit I am hard pressed to explain what is going on down there. I do not know. I am listening to it. I am there every day. I am watching it all unfold. It makes no sense to me.

Give them a free lunch and let them get out there, and we will call it our constituent assembly.

They then wrote books about it. Perhaps that was the downfall. Perhaps it was the downfall of the parliamentary system that someone wrote a book called Beauchesne and another guy wrote a book called Erskine May. Somehow these have become almost biblical in stature, rule books for a Parliament, and Parliament does not have to be relevant, it just has to follow those rules.

Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you that there is no doubt in my mind that when this bill comes up for my vote it is not going to get it, in case there is any doubt in anybody's mind.
I will tell you why. I have had very little difficulty in making up my mind on this. I want to explain to people just what is this disgusting, despicable Bill C-20 that everybody is talking about tonight? What does it do? How can one bill do so much damage to upset so many people? How can it?
It is very inoffensive. To describe it, it says: "Bill C-20, an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in Parliament on February 26, 1991". Aha, the budget of February 26, 1991.
It says it is going to amend certain statutes. There are two statutes which bother me, and I want to talk to them this evening.
The first one is the statute entitled the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act and the second one is the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I want to take a mythical couple in my riding. I can either put them at one end of the riding in Old Perlican, Grates Cove or Bay de Verde, beautiful little fishing villages in one end of my riding, or I can put them in the other end of my riding, the north end of my riding, up in Wesleyville, Valleyfield, Brookfield, Lumsden, Newtown, Templeman. I can put them in any of these places.
Let us take a couple and apply Bill C-20 to them and see how it is going to affect them. I want to say at the very beginning these are the people who in 1988, when I was going around campaigning with my opponents and other members of other parties, were listening to what we had to say. They were hearing the then sitting member from the party across the floor, the government party, saying: "Don't worry, be happy. Do not worry about all of this free trade business, this fear-mongering that Mifflin and his crowd are doing because nothing is going to happen to unemployment insurance. Mr. Cros-bie and the Prime Minister have given their word that nothing is going to happen. It is in the newspapers. Do not worry about that. Do not listen to those scare-mongers. When they say if you vote for this government and this free trade business, you are going to find yourself in a position where your credit card will be checked before your pulse is checked".
I never said that myself but that term was being used. I thought it was rather scary. Some people were saying that it would never happen, that it was scare-mongering and that no government would ever do that to its people. They said: "We have a system that if it was not there we would try to invent it. So because we have it we would not dare, even contemplate, getting rid of it".
The cost of education came up. There was no direct relationship between what was happening and the present cost of education but I think people, even then in 1988, knew that the cost of education would certainly not decrease and in all likelihood, as everything else had in the past four years, it would probably go up.
I want to mention the couples again in either end of my riding, put them in their mid-40s, give them three or four children, they are a working couple. Here is how I think it will affect them. I have to go back now and describe what this means in terms of money to the province I represent, the province of Newfoundland.
We do not have a very large budget in Newfoundland. The point is that half of that budget comes from the federal transfer payments in one way or another. We are very grateful to the government for that, I am not suggesting that we are ungrateful people. However, when practically half your budget comes from a certain source and that source has been cut dramatically then you are in trouble, particularly as it affects the three areas of unemployment insurance, post-secondary education-university education in other words-and health.
What can be more important to people of all ages?
In 1990 there was an announcement in the budget of that particular year that there would be a two-year freeze in federal transfer payments and that this freeze would cost Newfoundland $19 million in 1990 and $34 million in 1991-1992. That announcement was just last year. Nothing else had happened. That is what it would cost the province of Newfoundland.
In the last federal budget-and this is what we are talking about now, the effect that Bill C-20 has-the freeze was extended for another three years. If you take this freeze plus the freeze before, plus all the other freezes of the federal transfer payments and all the other various transfers to the province of Newfoundland, in the past six years since this government has been in power it will have cost Newfoundland a half a billion dollars by the end of 1992. In 1991-1992, this fiscal year alone, it will cost Newfoundland about $150 million. That is shameful. This is a very serious matter.

I have talked in general terms about the cost of education. What is our future in this country if we cannot afford to educate our children? What is the future? We know now we are behind the eight ball. We are behind the curve when it comes to the Europeans and the Japanese. We do not have our people educated properly. We are not going to improve the situation by increasing the cost of tuition, which is one of the results of Bill C-20, which we are going to effect this evening.
Let me talk about health right now.

Mr. Speaker, once more I rise to speak on the incredibly important and incredibly crucial matter of assistance from the federal government to the port of Halifax.
I am delighted to see the hon. member for Calgary Southeast who I presume is going to respond to this. Perhaps, I may be overly anticipating the hon. member in his reply, but I would like to put paid to the rumour here and now that the problems in the port of Halifax with most particular reference to the problems of container traffic and the weighing anchor of container companies away from Halifax to Montreal and other points is due to increased tonnage in the area.
This is something that I suspect was invented first by the Minister of Fisheries, has been picked up by the Minister of Transport, by the Associate Minister of Transport and most lately, by the Deputy Prime Minister in response to a question last week.
The president of the last container company to leave Halifax said explicitly and directly when asked: "Why are you going?", "The reasons are twofold: The first and foremost reason was the problem of freight rates between Halifax and Montreal. They were just not competitive." Consequently, we were losing business either to Montreal, within Canada or to the eastern ports of the United States, most of which interestingly enough are serviced by a railroad owned by Canadian Pacific which is, in itself, heavily subsidized and has been over the years by the federal government. The second problem cited by the president of that container company was the unfair tax structure yet again.
We do not ask for a great deal. We do ask for some action. We have asked for years that something be done
about the freight rates that are charged between Halifax and central Canada. We have asked again and again and again. What response have we received? One of the responses that we received is Bill C-ll, and in its former incarnation Bill C-26, the cancellation of the At and East grain subsidy. This is not the response that Haligonians and Nova Scotians are looking for. We are looking for some true action on the part of this government.
Four-and-a-half weeks ago in this House, the Minister of Transport told me, and I quote, as I quoted before, that he would: "do everything in his power to help the port of Halifax". On Friday last, the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada said: "We take this seriously. We take it as seriously as the member from Halifax does, and we are going to do something".
Several weeks ago I questioned the Associate Minister of Transport, and she, too, said something will be done. Sadly, what those comments remind me of, and what they remind Haligonians who have a sense of history of, were the words of the then King of England, Edward VIII, when he visited the coal fields in Wales and saw the unemployment. He said: "Something must be done".
What he did two weeks later was abdicate his responsibility. This government is abdicating its responsibility in and to the people of Halifax. Something has to be done, not mere words, not fine phrases. Assistance is needed and assistance is needed now for the Port of Halifax and for the people of Halifax.

The minister of privatization or whatever it is, says he is going for a drink. That would probably help his understanding. The member chose to intervene in the debate. The minister chose to heckle during the debate. There is no order in that point. It seems to me
that if the government members are interested in listening, I hope they will just learn a point of two from the observations we have to make.
This is one of the most important policy initiatives that is before the House in this part of the session. It represents a significant departure of Canadian policy which would permit the sale of automatic weapons to Saudi Arabia. That country has a very poor human rights record. It is in a region of the world which is sensitive, testy and has just come through one of the most difficult wars of this century. The people of that region are still paying the price.
The war that we have seen in the gulf is a war which both sides in this House can see was caused by the uncontrolled sale of arms by the western world to a region which did not need those arms. It seems to me that the first issue is an issue of conscience of all Canadians. I believe that Canadians find it very difficult to understand why it is that one of the first bills that this government introduces in this session is a bill to extend and expand the sale of arms after the eloquent statements which were made at the end of the gulf war.
As we went through this bill and through committee, I learned a thing or two about how the government works. It became very clear that instead of the conspiracy theory of operation it is the screw-up theory that really counts most of the time. This bill was an invention of the international trade side and those who are responsible for selling goods abroad. The export permit people in External Affairs and the trade minister are responsible for this bill, not the External Affairs minister who is responsible for disarmament and arms control, not the Prime Minister, but those who are responsible for industry.
The argument that is made in committee for this bill over and over again is the industrial argument. Here we have jobs. Here we have an industry. Let's sell them. Who cares what the purpose of the weapons are? Who cares that there are people who may be killed as a result of the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia? That is irrelevant.
We had an official from the minister's department who came before our committee and said that the only reason for this bill was industrial. There was no examination of the security reasons for this bill, there was no suggestion of the foreign policy reasons for this bill. What we had was simply a trade deal.
June 19, 1991

Surely, after everything that the world has seen in this century, the time has come to call a halt to arms sales. That is the first issue before the House.
The second issue is that this bill is flawed. The government has said over and over again that it complies with certain standards when it comes to the sale of arms. But its members refuse to agree to an amendment which would incorporate those standards in the legislation. The government has refused amendments which would require it to make the list of countries public to whom arms will be sold. It has refused those amendments. It has refused sunset clauses. It has refused to set out the reasons why we should be permitting sale of arms abroad. That is the second reason why we are against this bill.
The government was so anxious that this bill go through because there is at least one side of the government's head which understands that the defence industry is fundamentally a flawed industry. Around the world, the market for arms is fading. The third world can no longer afford arms. The market in the west is contracting. The cold war is over and investments which Liberal and Conservative governments have made in the arms industry are proving to be flawed investments.

sponsibilities. As a Quebecer, a Francophone and a Canadian, I would like to repeat what Laurier said: "We are French Canadians, but our country is not limited to the land we see from the Citadel Quebec. Our country is Canada. Our fellow citizens are not only those with French blood in their veins. Our fellow citizens are people of all races and tongues who came to this country driven by the misfortunes of war, by chance, or of their own free will."
September 24, 1991



In closing, I want to address a few comments to Canadians outside Quebec. I say to them that the Meech Lake Accord failed for many reasons. One reason was that it did not address the legitimate concerns of aboriginal peoples of the north and of western and Atlantic Canada. I was among those who said that changes and improvements were required.
For a constitution to succeed now the aspirations of aboriginal people, as well as the hope and dreams of the people of the north, west and the Atlantic provinces must be addressed. I have constantly said in Quebec- and I have paid a certain political price for it-that the needs and aspirations of the rest of Canada must be addressed in any constitutional reform package. I said we need a Canada round.
But I want to say to the rest of Canada that Quebec too has needs and aspirations which are legitimate and which must be met.

I have said repeatedly in Quebec-at considerable personal cost-that the needs and aspirations of all of Canada must be dealt with satisfactorily in any proposal for constitutional reform. However, I want to make it clear to Canada that Quebec also has needs and aspirations that are entirely legitimate and that must be satisfied.

I appeal to the values we share of tolerance and particularly of generosity. Let us use the next few months to understand that Quebec's distinctiveness makes Canada a greater country. Let us use the next few months to understand that the flourishing French fact across Canada helps us compete in a global society.
Let us use the next few months to understand that aboriginal self-government is a test of our values. Let us all demonstrate over the next few months thoughtfulness, reason, generosity, a willingness to accommodate and a skill to negotiate.
Let us get this constitutional issue behind us so that we can be equipped to deal with the real problems and challenges confronting us.
Routine Proceedings
There is nobody who has been obliged to talk more about the Constitution than I since 1980 so I hope that I will turn the page soon and that we will devote our attention to jobs, to competitiveness, to the environment, to health care, to make sure that we can take our proper place in the world of tomorrow.

Canada is inescapably a part of the global economy as a country whose prosperity depends on the export of almost 30 per cent of what it produces, about 50 per cent for agriculture. Canada has been actively participating in the Uruguay round negotiations for the past five years and has been pushing for a strengthened and balanced set of rules regarding agriculture. Canada will continue to do so.
A successful resolution of the MTN is one of Canada's highest trade priorities. It is founded on the simple principle that the fewer trade barriers there are between countries, the more prosperous these countries will be.
The current rounds of talks began in Uruguay in September 1986. We had high hopes that we would achieve breakthroughs in many fields, as for the first time agriculture was in the forefront of the discussions. It was this government that insisted that agriculture be at that forefront.

We want clearer and fairer GATT rules that apply equally to all countries, including a strengthened and clarified article XI, the elimination of a country's specific exemptions and better disciplines on the use of countervailing duties. Finally, we want to see the development of a framework of rules to prevent the abuse of health and sanitary regulations as disguised barriers to trade.
We have developed a balanced and comprehensive offer which is consistent with our objectives of substantial trade liberalization, fairer and more predictable trade rules, and equal treatment among GATT countries.
Canada's offer and objectives in the MTN remain unchanged.
We continue to pursue those objectives because we are convinced that an agreement which achieves them will be beneficial for all Canadian agriculture.
The clarification and strengthening of article XI remains a key objective for Canada. Our proposal, tabled last year, includes specific proposals for clarifying a country's rights and obligations through rules on product coverage for processed products, the meeting of effective supply control, the establishing of import access and new disciplines on exports. This balanced proposal was developed in close consultation with all sectors of Canadian agriculture and enjoys the support of the entire agrifood industry.
Canada has vigorously pursued the proposal of article XI, working with other countries including the EEC, Japan, Austria, Switzerland, Norway, Finland and Korea, which support the retention and clarification of article XI. Government Orders
We are debating this bill today because in May the Supreme Court of Canada struck down the previous law dealing with the criminally insane and ordered that new legislation be put into effect by November 2. The Supreme Court ruled that this system violated the rights of mentally ill people. It is estimated that about
1,100	people are currently being held on Lieutenant-Governor's warrants across the country. Bill C-30 proposes to match the period of incarceration to the crime. Madam Chairman, clause 14 is a new clause. It is not the normal clause that we have in back-to-work legislation.

October 10, 1991
Government Orders
We were not given any warning that the government would be changing this particular clause. Normally there is a guarantee with regard to back-to-work legislation that the employer and employees will have at least 12 hours after the act is proclaimed.
It was just last week that we had the situation with regard to the Public Service Alliance strike that the Senate, in its rush to pass the legislation, did so at five or six minutes to eight o'clock in the evening.
The President of the Treasury Board was on the air saying he expected people to be back at work at eight o'clock the next morning. He gave them 12 hours and six minutes, or something of that nature.
Of course that created great confusion because there was no way that a lot of people would even know that the Senate had passed the legislation at five minutes to eight o'clock in the evening.
I should point out that I was one of those people. I was called by some people who said: "When do we have to report back to work?" I did not know exactly when the Senate had passed the legislation.
There are absolutely no restrictions in this new amendment. There is not even a guarantee of 12 hours. It is quite possible that if the Senate in its rush tomorrow passes this legislation at four o'clock in the afternoon, the cabinet could say: "We want you people back at work one hour hence".
It was not that long ago that we guaranteed people 24 hours before they had to return to work. Then the last legislation said 12 hours. Now there is no given time, no minimum time. I suspect that the minister might get up and give assurances to this House that he will not do anything nefarious or he will not use the store alarm that the President of the Treasury Board tried to use.
On the other hand, I would not like to see this clause, even if we get assurances at this time, used in the future. It gives too much power to the government with absolutely no guarantees that either the employees or employers will have adequate information and adequate time to do it as required.

Madam Speaker, I have the opportunity this evening to rise in response to a question that I posed in this House to the Prime Minister on October 2 that had to do with the rate of child poverty in this country.
I thought perhaps at the time that the Prime Minister had unintentionally misconstrued what I was asking in my question because of the response I got from him in which he said I was trying to mislead the Canadian public and was giving false information.
I tabled information in this House which corroborated the statement I made which was that there are more than one million children living in poverty in this country. I say that I thought that perhaps I had been misinterpreted and gave the Prime Minister the benefit of the doubt. I was frankly appalled by a response I got to my question from the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which he critiqued what I had said in the document that had been tabled in the House.
Subsequently I have been in touch with many of the agencies that deal with those living in poverty in this country and particularly children. In 1990 Statistics Canada tells us that there were 5.6 million children under the age of 14 years living in Canada. Those human beings who are aged 15, 16, 17 and 18 are also considered to be children in this country. One in six children today is estimated to be living in poverty in this country. That makes more than one million children living in poverty in this country. It is a dreadful legacy that we leave for the future of this country to permit such a thing to exist.
Beyond just the argument over statistics and numbers, I was very concerned with what the Minister of National Health and Welfare was saying in his letter. At one point he stated that we should be proud of certain statistics about Canadian initiatives and other federal initiatives that have been taken vis-a-vis children.
For example, the government has made a dollar commitment to eliminating the problem of family violence. That is very important and we support that. We know that the situation of poverty contributes to family violence in this country and the government is not facing the reality of how children are living in this country.
I certainly am affronted by the response and the attitude of this government. It is not only myself. There
are many people who care for children and their future in this country and our country's future is our children today. The government will hear more from me and those agencies on this issue in the coming days.

Yes, it helps unite the country, as the hon. member said. Mr. Speaker, not only does small business create 75 per cent of the jobs and help regional development, but without it, regional development would be impossible and small municipalities across Canada would have trouble surviving.
This is just one more reason why the government should consider this question and revise all the rules that existed in the past. I heard some ideas put forward in the House by the government, the NDP and by our own party. All these ideas contain some useful elements, but I think we have to take a radical position. We have to say: Listen, we are convinced, and we need only look at the evidence of the past few years, especially the last ten or fifteen, that small business is the most important motor of our economy. Once we have set aside all the rules we had in the past, we can advance with leaps and bounds. We will take radical steps to ensure that small business gets all the help it needs to develop.
Mr. Speaker, there are solutions, and this was in consultation with the CPQ. First, it is necessary to have loans to promote small business. No handouts, no grants. Small business wants the government to make available or guarantee loans so it can get started. This is one of the most important aspects of developing small business, in other words, ensuring funds are available.
Of course, we don't expect the government or the banks to give small business a blank cheque. There is a certain process, as the CPQ explained, and I understand that. Second, know the market, which is only common sense; third, know your product, and then know the best
ways to market it. There are experts in this area so the expertise is there. Of course there is also the question of economic feasibility.
As for the criteria, if small business, if entrepreneurs and beginning entrepreneurs meet these four criteria- and there might be others, of course-but if they can meet these four criteria, they will be prepared to face the competition. They will be productive and competitive. But if they don't get a chance -You cannot make something out of nothing. They need this help. I think that was one of the elements emphasized by the CPQ.
Mr. Speaker, let's not forget training. This is a key element. Without training, you will not get anywhere. There is a debate taking place in France at this very moment, which I am following very closely, and I say this for the benefit of our listeners. The French Minister of Education has realized that training has become extremely important in a highly competitive world where the word productivity is sacred. The French Education Minister said that unfortunately, the French are not like the Germans. As you know, the Germans have a great tradition in their country of apprenticeship schools, technical schools and trade schools. They are the best in this respect.
So the French are starting to realize how important this is and that they also need technical schools and training schools and apprenticeship systems. They have to find industries that are willing to make a major contribution to training. In Germany, industries set the curriculum because they pay for these technical schools, to a considerable extent. Now that is a sensible idea we could use here in Canada. You wouldn't think we had relations with Germany! If the French with their reputation for being inventive and innovative, a reputation they have had for centuries, feel they must look to the German experience which has been extremely positive, we in Canada could also benefit by using this approach to train our labour force.
When we have that kind of training, when governments realize the importance of involving small business, I am sure the banks will sit up and take notice, that risk taking will become a normal thing for entrepreneurs in

the small business community and that job creation will be enhanced for the greater benefit of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I too welcome you back after a month and a half absence due to your operations.
With too many of the 52 languages of the aboriginal peoples of Canada eroded or lost, any serious attempt to reinvigorate their languages must be worth while. I salute the member for Western Arctic on the bill, as I believe most members in the House today do as well.
Linguistic relativity emphasizes the unique role of language in relation to culture. Language is recognized as a means far more than mere communication. It is a vehicle of cultural transmission. For some renowned scholars like Benjamin Whorf language even shapes thought and emotion, determining the perception of reality. Although not identical the concepts of language and culture are inseparable. To put it more plainly, I am told by my colleague that there are numerous official languages in the Northwest Territories. That is why I understand there is excellent language harmony in the north. They can have unilingual MLAs and unilingual jurors. This growing recognition of all languages in the north is working well.

Private Members' Business
There are nine official languages in the European community. The chief quoted by my colleague has said: "Language is the heart of our culture".
You will recall, Sir, being from Edmonton, that children sent to residential schools returned home often unable to communicate with their parents and grandparents because of the loss of their aboriginal language skills and the almost total disorientation of their cultural value system. The educational system of those days did much more than to exert strong pressure on aboriginal children. Again, Sir, I remind you that our aboriginal peoples came to Canada at least 13,000 years ago. The residential schools fostered an intergenerational culture gap in aboriginal communities. Many young people have suffered from the in between feeling of not being able to fit in either their home communities or communities elsewhere.
Aboriginal peoples resented what was being done to them and tried to resist as best they could the efforts to damage their way of life. They still do and continue to do so, in Ovide Mercredi's words, "to break the psychology of domination from the two founders of the nation".
The cultural resurgence and the defence of territory are but two overt expressions of native self-determination. Other forms of resistance have included economic and political action, the reinterpretation of historical events, the formation of intertribal and interdenominational networks, and so on.
Since 1867 and earlier, aboriginal groups have actively sought recognition of their inherent right to self-government. This right was exercised thousands of years before Europeans arrived on this continent. Many believe it has never been extinguished. Certainly my party does. Claims that political structures were unknown to native people prior to contact with Europeans ignore the fact that most First Nations had complex forms of government that go back centuries. In fact, aboriginal self-government is now supported in principle by most Canadians., happily, who believe that recognizing the role of aboriginal peoples in Confederation is very important for national pride.
Canadians have a chance to demonstrate to the world that the old notions of European dominance are gone. In our country we see federalism as a way of protecting the
identity of minorities. Federalism is practised throughout the world in large measure to provide and respect the identity of minority regions and peoples.
The encouragement of cultural development assists in preserving and strengthening aboriginal peoples integrity. A stronger sense of cultural worth would promote aboriginal self-sufficiency as one of the proclaimed goals of our country. Dependency on the other hand tends to alienate aboriginal peoples and all peoples from their traditional identity and prevents the retention of some features of traditional culture. Only with the maintenance of a distinct identity can our aboriginal peoples have the chance, as was indicated earlier by the member for the Western Arctic, of altering the wider conditions of social and economic dependency which so characterized much of their lives now.
To this end it seems to me that the importance of language retention far exceeds the magnitude of retention of other features of traditional culture. Language retention contributes to the maintenance of the boundary between the aboriginal peoples and others. As a mode of communication, it is a system of meaningful signs that represent and influence the concept of the world.
According to one critic, language retention is the cultural characteristic that best reflects current and continued cultural cohesion. It is perhaps the most distinctly ethnic activity.
I am fast running out of time and I do not want, Mr. Speaker, to be talking when this bill stands in danger of being talked out. Let me quote from the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation which asserted: "No single feature of southern culture was as profound in its effects on the Inuit way of life as television. It destroyed old habits and social behaviours. It imported new values and attitudes. It became an alternative way of life, particularly for the young".
There is an urgent need for more not less funding for native aboriginal media and aboriginal languages so that they can continue to reach aboriginal communities to provide material dealing with contemporary issues as well as traditional cultures, particularly so that they can develop children's content.


If no action is taken such as proposed here, linguists and anthropologists will mourn the passing of aboriginal languages and in consequence, aboriginal cultures. It is largely up to the aboriginal peoples themselves to decide whether it is in their interest to allow their languages to fade into disuse or to revive them. If they choose the latter, they will deserve the support of all Canadians.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join my colleagues in congratulating you and welcoming you back in your House. We are extremely happy to see you back in such a great shape. You bring some sort of personal warmth to this place and it gives me pleasure to mention this.
Mr. Speaker, it is with both humility and great pride that I take part in this debate on Bill C-282 put forward by our colleague from Western Arctic.
Mr. Speaker, many members, in fact most of us have read this bill and it is obvious that we each want to speak in support of it.
When you look at its purpose, this bill does the Parliament of Canada, as well as this social reality of our beautiful country, great credit. It talks about promotion, providing information, developing programs, assisting in the production, with each new item reinforcing and providing new ways of making Canada what it is, different from any other country and of course from our neighbour to the south.
As President of the Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship, I also have the duty and the pleasure to look at this matter and participate in the debate. Mr. Speaker, as some members pointed out, this bill deals with the very fabric of our nation. Parliament and its members are asked to consider, work on and pass a bill which ensures that every Canadian citizen has the pleasure and privilege of reverting to his or her mother tongue and thus rediscover, if they were lost or not as lively as they could be, his or her roots and integrity.


Private Members' Business
The mother tongue, Mr. Speaker, is not only a symbol. It is also a social reality, but even more so a psychological reality. The child starts learning on his mother's lap how to grow up into an adult, to develop, to grow richer with a full scale of values and these, of course, will be transmitted through language.
I think that the mother tongue is the noblest symbol and reflection of our lives in our society. Language is associated to the first cries, the first laughs and words of a child, as he or she starts to develop, to relate with their environment, their country. The loss of this language would necessarily mean the loss of part of their roots and it could take them several years of efforts to regain that sense of belonging, of wholeness fundamental to any nation.
For a number of weeks now, Mr. Speaker, I have been wondering about a couple of concepts. The first one is the concept of national unity which I relate to the concern for and the concept of national identity.
And I wonder whether we can find several national identities through this same unity. I found an article by Claude Levi-Strauss and Didier Eribon in last January's issue of L'Actualite, and I would like to tell you about it.
Levi-Strauss wrote: "It is better that cultures remain diverse or that they renew themselves through diversity. However, one must be willing to pay the price: namely, that cultures linked to a particular lifestyle or value system must protect their distinctive characteristics; such a situation is healthy, and not at all, as some would have us believe, pathological. Each culture evolves through a process of give and take with other cultures. However, each culture must offer some resistance; otherwise, it would soon have nothing of its own to give in return."
Mr. Speaker, Levi-Strauss is not just anybody- my colleague is laughing at that and that makes me relax a bit because these issues concern me very deeply. As I was saying, Levi-Strauss is not just anybody: He is certainly a first-class author.
Following what I was reading, I wrote that, for a number of years now, this question of unity, this question of identity, is a source of concern within organizations and businesses. And, without going back too far, it is interesting to note that the second industrial revolution prepared industry to have to deal with the problem. Companies were growing and expanding and the craftsman was forced more and more to fit into a larger entity
and risked losing his identity. Pretty soon after this second revolution, there came this author, Fayol, and this philosophy of the Protestant ethic, that emphasized unity of command and organizational unity. Therefore, the individual, caught in this organization's tentacles, would often wonder whether he was losing his identity.
Then came McLuhan and other authors from sociology and psychology. They examined this issue with a much more scientific approach, so that in the 1950s William White came out with a book and a theory called "The Organization Man". White told us that workers suppressed their identity. The greater the proliferation of organizations, the more important it is for the individual to find reference points and deep roots. Mr. Speaker, as you know, it is through language, the mother tongue, that a culture can regain its roots and be reborn. That is why, as committee chairman, and also because our minister, who is responsible for multiculturalism, allocates money, but more importantly, implements a philosophy to protect all these cultural assets.
Mr. Speaker, I understand my time is up.

Mr. Speaker, since this is the first time I have had a chance to speak in debate with you in the Chair since your return, on behalf of my wife and three daughters whom you know very well I would like to welcome you back. Everyone agrees the bill is an improvement over what is in place now but there are still some problems.
The bill as it now stands provides no protection for the primary producers like the farmers and fishermen. The sad state of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada is obvious in the number of processing plant bankruptcies.
The farming industry is going through some tough times and those people are going out of business as well.
The long and the short of the matter is that the economy is in such a mess because of this government's policies that we need a new Bankruptcy Act to deal with the situation.
I have fishermen in my riding who have lost thousands of dollars because the processor they dealt with went under. Fishermen sell their fish expecting to get paid for their work, but when fish companies go broke, they cannot collect a dime. This is just not acceptable.
In this bill there is a clause dealing with unpaid suppliers. It says that unpaid suppliers can go in after a company declares bankruptcy and retrieve their goods for up to 30 days. However, to do this a number of conditions must be met. The product must be in original condition and must be identifiable from other products.
For farmers and fishermen this is a very serious problem. Anyone who knows anything about fishing knows that you cannot tell one lobster from another in a crate. As well, lobsters that are processed are processed immediately, changing the condition of the lobster. Under the current proposals the fisherman would be out of luck and still would not be able to collect a cent. This is just not acceptable.
Similarly, in the farming industry there is no way I can tell a potato of the same variety that I grow from my neighbour's up the road who grows potatoes. All potatoes of the same variety as we well know look the same. In the fall a farmer usually sells his product to a single wholesaler or processor. It that company goes broke, the farmer cannot get anything back.
What many people do not realize is that a bankruptcy does not affect only one company or one person. In one processor bankruptcy a fisherman in my riding lost $30,000 and to a fisherman in my riding, that is a big loss and a lot of money. Fishermen have to pay their helpers, make payments on their boats, pay for bait and pay for many things. The $30,000 that was not paid to one fisherman ends up coming out of the pockets of many people. Thirty thousand dollars is a person's income for a year. In bankruptcy that is the same thing as losing your job.
These are the serious reasons why fishermen and farmers need protection. When a company goes bank-

rupt many people get hurt. For some time I have been trying to get some protection for farmers and fishermen who are affected by bankruptcies.
I wrote to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans asking him to help fishermen. The best the minister said he could do was talk to his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and see if it could be put in the Bankruptcy Act revisions. That was almost a year ago. We now have the government's revisions and there is still no protection for farmers and fishermen.
I and my colleague from Dartmouth and other members of the Liberal Party have been trying to make changes to Bill C-22. An amendment has to be put forward that will allow fishermen to retrieve goods from a bankrupt company after the value has been added. This gives greater protection to fishermen. Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for his question. It is a very important question.
The issue is really what secured creditors would pay the super priority. When there are specific charges, for example a mortgage on real estate, a mortgage or a conditional sales contract on piece of machinery or a specific assignment of a specific receivable, clearly those specific assignments or specific agreements come first and are not subject to any priority, because the person who has those specific agreements has the right above the receiver or above the trustee in bankruptcy in the same manner as a landlord exercising his landlord's lien has a claim above the trustee or receiver.
The issue on which you claim here then is the floating charge type, unassigned or unspecifically assigned assets.
Since the last Bankruptcy Act, banks and other lenders to companies have found that they can register in Canada, though not in the United States. They can register floating charge security. This bill like all legislation is based on a principle but it is also an attempt to define and put into place regulations that attempt to bring the principle to life. While I support the principle and general thrust of Bill C-22 there are in my opinion a number of ways to greatly improve the legislation.
I would like to offer a couple of suggestions which I believe were also made in committee. First, there is the issue of priority in cases of bankruptcy. Bill C-22 does not really give jurisdictional priority to workers. It does not challenge the traditional hierarchy of creditors. The only wage claim payment contained in the bill is in fact external to the bankruptcy settlements process. It comes in the form of employer tax to be collected through the system.
What this government is doing is getting some additional taxation by passing a bill and again hitting the very people who are going to have the hardest time in trying to pay, and that is the small business people and the various small businesses which are trying to operate in very competitive markets.
Yet the government is determined to bring in this kind of taxation that will bring about those kinds of problems. For instance, it does not address the issue of private pensions. What about the pensions within the protection of a bankruptcy act. People have paid into pensions, or are part of a private pension scheme. While we look at the protection of the wage portion of it, what about the pensions? I say to you that while we are addressing the kind of work that went into this kind of bill, that is this big and this thick, and with all the committee work that went on, surely the government could have considered protecting pensions also. There are some very serious flaws in this bill.

As well, the $60 million wage compensation fund which is supposed to cover all of Canada is a band-aid. This fund will be eaten up in no time at all if the present levels of bankruptcies continue.
In my riding alone, I know of many bankruptcies that have taking place and of the serious affects they have, not only on the workers but also the people who are losing their pensions. It also hurts the surrounding community.
Finally on this point, the tax of 10 cents per week per worker is unfair. Surely we should take into account the size and health of the business. Should a small business really be taxed at the same rate as, let us say, the finance industry which employs 500,000 people? Should municipal governments, hospitals or school boards be forced to pay this tax when they cannot go bankrupt?
I feel these are questions that should be looked at seriously before the final bill is passed.
The idea of establishing priority for workers would have many advantages over a fund created by a new tax. By giving employees priority over banks the legislation would be practically self-financing.
In most cases banks are the first in line to collect outstanding debts during bankruptcy. It is common practice for banks to ensure that the market value of assets pledged as collateral is much less than the size of the loans. Why not give employees a priority? Who would lose? things that are added into this bill and some of the things that are going on in this bill makes it almost impossible for me to do so.

Every bill we see in this House is further taxation. For goodness sake, get away from this idea of taxation and find another way that is more evenly balanced and fairer for our people.

Mr. Speaker, I must say something about these insignificant amendments proposed by the minister. My colleague from Rosemont, and particularly the hon. member for Saint-Hubert, have both examined this bill in detail and they spent many hours listening to different groups across Canada, especially from Quebec. I want to congratulate them because their convictions did not change when they changed affiliation. As far as I know, the value of life is the same, whether one lives in the country or in the city. The same emotions are stirred and the same troubles ensue when firearms are misused in the city or in the country. A bullet is as deadly in the city as it is in the country.
When I hear this so-called lobby claim that it speaks on behalf of rural Canada, I am sorry but I think the problem is being misplaced. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this amendment of the Liberal member for Kenora-Rainy River. He would
eliminate the enabling power in this legislation for the minister to ban large capacity magazines of the type Marc Lepine used in Montreal.
The bill creates the enabling power to ban large capacity magazines through regulation. It is not done in the bill. It is going to be done by regulations. The minister, however, has indicated that she is going to propose the prohibiting of all handgun magazines that hold more than 10 centre fire cartridges and all magazines for semi-automatic long guns that hold more than five centre fire cartridges. That is what she proposes to do. The question then is: What about competition shooters? There is a legitimate objection. We have amended the bill so that there is a specific exemption for legitimate competition shooters. They need not worry.
There has been concern expressed by some firearms groups that the magazine size would apply to rifles they already have. An example would be the bolt action Lee-Enfield. An extremely rare semi-automatic rifle called the Charlton may use the Lee-Enfield magazine. The concern was that the Lee-Enfield would be caught up in the prohibition because of the possible use of the magazine in the Charlton.
I put this question specifically to the minister. The minister and the parliamentary secretary assured me directly that there was a commitment that the Lee-Enfield would not be affected. I think that disposes of two objections right there.
It seems to me that the member is wrong. It is ironic that he is opposing the proposal to ban high capacity magazines, because high capacity magazines surely are not needed for hunting. Legitimate hunters do not need high capacity magazines. They are used more in assault weapons.
It is true that some legitimate shooting competitions, particularly handguns, use large capacity magazines but that issue is addressed as I said with the exemption. As a member of the BQ said, Lepine used a 30-round magazine at the Ecole Polytechnique massacre. Three weeks ago in Texas, at that horrific massacre there, there was the use of a 17-round magazine.
Why ban large capacity magazines? Let us deal with the real issue. A ban on large capacity magazines is a
November 5, 1991

practical way of limiting fire power. "Fire power", to quote a background paper prepared for the special committee on Bill C-80, "is a combination of cartridge power, possible rate of fire and ammunition capacity". Limiting the size of a magazine is a reasonable alternative to banning semi-automatic weapons. Many semi-automatic weapons have common and legitimate uses in Canada. Rather than banning the weapon, the government has chosen to limit the fire power of semi-automatics in a way that will not interfere with hunting.
That is really the key and that is why I am opposing the Liberal motion and supporting this provision in the bill. There is a problem with an increase in firepower weapons in Canada. There must be a way of addressing such weapons that are already in the hands of Canadians.
In recent years a large number of military firearms have been in Canada from a number of eastern European and Third World countries in search of foreign currency. For example, the Norinco AK-47, a Chinese copy of the Soviet assault rifle, can be bought in Montreal for $450 according to the evidence we had in our committee.
This provision will limit the capacity of future firearms' design. Weapons are becoming more and more dangerous all the time. Even if the magazine proposal has a limited impact on existing weapons, it will have the effect of stopping future, unnecessary innovation and advanced fire power before they become a problem. It seems to me that is sufficient reason to support the proposal.
I want to close with two concerns that the member from Kenora had. It has been argued that the limit of five on semi-automatic rifles will affect built-in magazines. Images of thousands of rifles having to be destroyed have been put forward by the gun lobby. So hundreds get concerned: "My God, my gun is going to be destroyed". In fact evidence presented to our special committee suggested that in 1991 of approximately 2,600 makes and models of rifles only 28 would be affected. Some 26 of these guns are in the paramilitary class and would be prohibited or restricted in any event. Thus, of 2,600 guns only two versions of the Marlin Camp Carbine are affected. For this the Liberal member from Kenora wants to eliminate an important element of the bill. It seems to me he has not thought it through.
Government Orders
Groups have raised the issue of magazines that can be used in semi-automatic and non semi-automatic firearms. Only one firearm, the Lee-Enfield, has been identified as a problem, and I already explained how I put this question to the minister.
I listened to what the member said and I think he addressed some concerns, but I think they have been dealt with. We try to deal with them in amendments we fought for in the bill, and we got them. As I said, the alternative would be to ban semi-automatics. The government has chosen not to do that. Legitimate hunters do not need large clips. Competition shooters are exempt and so I think the amendment should fall.

Madam Speaker, the correctional institution at Haney was in its day one of the leading institutions in Canada. The first warden of the place is probably still kicking around in the federal correctional system.

It aimed at treatment of offenders from age 14 to 25. The oldest individual was 25. At one point we had somebody who was 40 and was very carefully selected before being allowed to go there. It usually involved special training and education.
Most of the crime in society is committed by younger people. Some of the worst crimes that I have ever heard of, or had the misfortune to open the folders on, were committed by teenagers who wound up in that institution. At the beginning it was a school for the penitentiary. There were incredible tragedies in the place. It was basically young offenders inflicting the kinds of things I was talking about on other young offenders.

On an afternoon or night shift after program we were looking at eight staff for 500 inmates. I can remember being left in the movie theatre with seven other colleagues and 500 inmates. There were not enough staff to cover the lights and the projection room. We were locked in and there were four other staff and the administrator outside patrolling the outside areas. When the order in the dark broke down there were eight of us and 500 inmates.
I was under the impression that they were going to be peeling us off the wall by the time the RCMP finally got in and broke it up. When you are dealing with effective working staff ratios of 100 to 1 you cannot do anything effective. In many cases you need the leaders of the unit to assist you in keeping it running. That is a common technique staff use to survive.
