Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to rise and speak in favour of this bill at third reading stage. I believe this bill represents a major improvement in the law respecting the mentally disordered who have come into conflict with the criminal law.
In introducing this bill the Minister of Justice said it proposes "wide-ranging changes to modernize, streamline and clarify the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with mentally disordered accused".
Today I would like to deal with the role of the review boards in assuring that mentally disordered persons who have been found to be either unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible are dealt with fairly and in a manner that takes into account public safety.
Under the provisions of the Criminal Code as they stand today, the lieutenant-governor of the province is the person responsible for making all decisions regarding the detention, care and conditions of release of those under the authority of a lieutenant-governor's warrant. While the code does provide for the establishment of boards to review the cases of persons held in custody under a lieutenant-governor's warrant, this provision is not mandatory. British Columbia and the two territories have yet to establish review boards under the authority of the code. The role of the board is merely advisory. Nor
does the code give much guidance as to how boards should conduct themselves.
It is therefore not surprising that the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its report entitled Mental Disorder in the Criminal Process, published in 1976, found that the make-up of the boards differ, the resources available to the boards differ, the criteria they apply, the procedures they use, the material they examine and the rights they accord the prisoner patients all differ from province to province. In some the differences far exceed the similarities.
While in recent years the review boards have taken pains to find out what their counterparts in other provinces are doing, the first annual report, Canadian Data Base: Patients Held On Lieutenant-Governors' Warrants, prepared by Doctors Hodgins and Webster for the federal Department of Justice in October 1989, continued to show very considerable discrepancies in procedures.
I do not by this intend any criticism of the review boards or their members who are performing a difficult task with great dedication. Nor am I suggesting that we should insist upon absolute uniformity of procedure as between the various review boards. However it behoves us to assure that there is equality of justice in the way in which we treat mentally disordered persons who come into conflict with the criminal law. This is particularly so in light of the comments made by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Swain v. The Queen, which talks about the way in which mentally disordered individuals are dealt with presently under the Criminal Code.
In order to foster equality of treatment the bill requires that a review board be set up in each province and territory. This provision guarantees that no matter where one is in Canada cases of this type will be dealt with by a body that has the same structure, powers and obligations as elsewhere in the country. Moreover, henceforth the review board will be the decision-making body rather than merely an adviser to the lieutenant-governor as is the case today.
From both a legal and practical point of view this change makes sense. There is a principle of law that the person who decides the case must hear the evidence, but the lieutenant-governor presently hears neither the witnesses nor the arguments of counsel. It is the review board that sees the mentally disordered person, hears

the evidence, examines the files and has the expertise to make a proper assessment of what needs to be done.
From a practical point of view in the larger provinces if the lieutenant-governor were to consider each individual's case with the same care that the review boards do, he or she would have to spend almost full time examining and deciding these cases. Of necessity therefore the lieutenant-governor must rely on the recommendations of the review board. The proposed modification puts the decision-making powers where they belong.
This bill also proposes changes in the structure of the review boards. Under the existing provisions of the Criminal Code, a review board shall consist of a minimum three and a maximum of five members, at least two of whom shall be duly qualified psychiatrists entitled to engage in the practice of medicine under the laws of the province for which the board is appointed, and one member shall be a member of the bar of that province.

The membership of the review boards will also be changed. He said: Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to lead the debate on third reading of this bill.
Bill C-3 is the cornerstone for a new regime of real property management by the government. This new regime will improve services to the public. It will improve internal government efficiencies and it will bring real property conveyancing by the government into the modem era.
I would like to take a few moments to summarize some of the main features of this bill. First, Bill C-3 is designed to be the primary authority for real property
transactions by the federal government. The existing legislation in this area no longer creates a unified framework for real property transactions. Bill C-3 would consolidate the three main real property statutes into one act, with one framework and one set of rules.
Second, Bill C-3 would simplify and modernize real property management and conveyance practices by the government. The current statutes have been essentially unchanged for some time and do not allow the use of modem real property methods or practices. Even a transaction involving a small piece of property can take much longer to complete than would be normal in the private sector. Bill C-3 would improve this situation.
This bill would also permit the use of conveyancing practices commonly used within the private sector, thus making it easier to deal with the federal government. We will be able to carry out a real property transaction in a province in a way familiar to the people of that province. This will make transactions by the government not only more efficient but also simpler and more understandable by the public.
Bill C-3 has been designed so that it would not affect real property governed by special program legislation such as the National Parks Act or the Territorial Lands Act. Bill C-3 is a residual statute and its provisions would be overridden by specialized legislation.
Finally this bill would clarify the role of Treasury Board to manage more effectively real property conveyancing. Mr. Speaker, I think you have to understand what is envisaged by this particular motion. We on this side of the House have taken the position that banks should do the things that banks best know how to do and that insurance companies should do the things related to insurance matters. Similarly, trust companies should do the things related to trust and loan companies, and co-operatives in the same fashion.
We have opposed every attempt to collapse the pillars. When this bill is all done it is going to allow banks to own insurance companies, insurance companies to own trust and loan companies, and banks to own trust and loan companies. I have no hesitation in saying that when this is all passed you are going to see the greatest urge to merge ever in this countiy.
We have taken the position that we ought not to go for that approach. The sumo wrestler approach is not the one that we should be aiming for. We have said that there is nothing wrong with a bank entering into an agreement with an insurance company, a joint venture, and for the bank to market the insurance products of an insurance company or several insurance companies. Already banks do insure. There is creditor insurance and banks do market insurance. There is mortgage insurance and banks do market mortgage insurance. We have said quite frankly to banks: "You cannot market insurance out of your branches, but you can go ahead and set up your own insurance company or buy one of the smaller insurance companies and start building its base".
It seems to me that this is not serving the interests of consumers. All this will lead to when it is all said and done is that one morning Canadians are going to wake up and there will only be one super financial institution with arms like an octopus.
When we dealt with Bill C-83, which is the former name of C-4 in the previous Parliament, we came to clause 416 and lo and behold we looked at the French version of the clause and the French version says that you cannot do anything except what we tell you to do. I moved to change the French version so that it was more consistent with the English version. All the members on the committee agreed to that.
I want to say that the beloved chairman of our committee flew off to Toronto and spoke to a meeting of insurance brokers and insurance companies.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the naivety of the previous speaker is overwhelming on two points. This amendment is not primarily to try to keep executive salaries down. That is a matter for the various corporations to wrestle with. As far as the chief executive officers of one company not knowing approximately what the salaries of the chief executive officers of another company are, this is absolutely ridiculous. Of course they know. They do not know down to the exact penny or dollar or hundreds of dollars, but they certainly have a very clear idea of approximately what the top directors and the top CEOs are getting. As a matter of fact, if their stock is traded on any of the American exchanges all they have to do is phone Washington and they can find out immediately.
The point here is that it is a matter of principle. I do not know why there should be boardroom secrecy on this kind of issue. I do not know why we write laws in this country deliberately prohibiting or denying shareholders the right to know what their chief executives are earning. It is as simple as that. It is a matter of principle. It is a matter of openness.
I want to give an example of what happened in my community a number of years ago when the Canadian government and the government of the province of Ontario gave Massey-Ferguson Corporation $200 million in an attempt to get that company back on its feet; $125 million from the federal government and $75 million from the province of Ontario.
November 25, 1991

We in Brantford wanted to know what the then chief executive officer of that company was earning and we could not find out and the Government of Canada could not find out and the government of Ontario could not find out. Yet taxpayers were being asked to cough up $200 million to bail out that company. We had to go to the United States to find out what Victor Rice was earning. If memory serves me correctly I think he had taken a decrease in pay from something like $275,000 a year to $245,000 a year as his great contribution in helping to bail out that company at the same time that the taxpayers were giving him $200 million.
It is a matter of principle. We believe in an open society in this country. We believe in open government, although not all parties practice what they preach when it comes to open government. Here we have a wonderful opportunity in this House, legislatively, to make certain that shareholders and the general public and the Government of Canada know what the salaries of these chief executive officers are.
The other point is it is manifestly clear that chief executive officers do not want their employees to know and do not want their shareholders to know what their increases are year over year, when in periods of economic recession their employees are being asked to take less. There is the other side of the sword. Maybe some chief executive officers in the last couple of years have only had a 4 per cent or 5 per cent increase. Maybe some have had a 7 per cent or 8 per cent increase. If you add their perks and their privileges and the stocks that they get and the entire package then you may find that they are getting a hell of a lot more than 4 per cent or 5 per cent increases year over year during a recession when they are demanding from their employees maybe a 2 per cent or 3 per cent increase or maybe a 0 per cent increase.
Why not the openness? Why is the government defending the chief executive officers of the major financial institutions of this country against their own employees? That is the question and that is the principle.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, amendment 42A. which states that trust companies should have two auditors was actually discussed in the finance committee. This amendment that we have before us this morning actually contradicts the decision that was made in the finance committee which would allow a trust company to choose whether it needed one auditor or two.
Under the existing legislation, trust companies have one auditor. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the finance committee, as I mentioned a minute ago, felt that there was no obvious reason why we should require trust companies to have two auditors. In fact, as the hon. member for Mississauga has stated, and it was also indicated in the finance committee, there is a possibility if you have two that one auditor could believe that the other auditor was doing something that he is not and things could get missed. The hon. member for Nickel Belt mentioned the Estey inquiry which looked into the failure of the Canadian Bank and the Northland Bank. I want to remind him that Mr. Estey stated in that inquiry that the auditor system of having two auditors would not have made any difference at all to these two banks. Why would chartered banks want to have two auditors. That makes work. We also have to remember that auditors cost money and really, who is going to end
up paying the price tag? It is the customer or the trust company.
If I felt that it was absolutely necessary that a trust company should have two auditors, then certainly I would vote for this amendment. Obviously, from what we heard in the finance committee, and as I said, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions does not see any reason for this, I do not see any reason why we should inflict this cost on the Canadian public. If it is an unnecessary cost, why make the trust company customers pay for it?
I repeat, this was brought up in the finance committee. We voted against it. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions does not see any reason for it so, therefore, I will be voting against it.

changed: the way we ran our transport system, the way we ran our health care system and you name it. I had no idea that I lived in such an abominable society, that it needed to be so radically altered and so radically Americanized.

This is a deep, deep psycho-political sickness on the part of the government and it reaches into everything. Everything is being touched by this sickness of having to imitate. Let us get rid of anything that is Canadian, anything that worked and that made, in this case, for a very sound financial system, one of the soundest in the world. My God, it is an embarrassment. We are not a place where people can be real greedy guts, they can only be half greedy guts so, let us change it.
I just do not understand it and I find this whole mess the government is entering into here to be just another symptom of this malaise that unfortunately affects the whole country. If the Conservatives just want to bring themselves down it would not be so bad, but they are taking a very good country with them.

He said: Mr. Speaker, these two amendments would require two auditors for these new creatures that are being created with this legislation.
One of the things we have said consistently about these bills C-4, C-19 and C-28, is that they will result in a different kind of financial institution. Since the pillars are being collapsed in effect, insurance companies are going to own trust and loan companies.
There are expanded powers for insurance companies. They will be able to take certain types of deposits. They want to grow. They want to become bigger. They want to become global competitors.
As this happens we need to build in fail safe protection for depositors, investors and the people of Canada. I could not imagine why the government and the Liberal opposition would agree to reduce the number of auditors for a bank to one when they had two. I could not understand it.
I have heard the arguments from the member for Mississauga South and from the Liberal side. Having two auditors in the case of the Northland Bank and so on did not prevent the collapse of the bank. Because somebody broke into your house does not mean that you do not keep locks on the doors. That is the same argument.
Because people can break into your house, somehow or other you should make it easy for them and unlock the door. Leave it unlocked. We have argued that two auditors are essential. This is a check on what one auditor does. This is a protection for those who invest in the company and depositors.
I was amazed that the government members and the Liberal opposition in committee would actually vote to remove the dual auditor system. Yet they are prepared to put in the actuary and an auditor. It seems to me that the two auditors to check and double check on a financial institution is absolutely essential to the integrity of the institution.
We had evidence when Michael Mackenzie came before the committee on Standard Trust. If you read the evidence he gave-I read some of it into the record the other day-in the minutes of the finance committee meeting, he consistently pointed out how much OSFI depended on the auditor's report.
Government Orders
It consistently pointed out that OSFI does not have the wherewithal to do the audit of all the financial institutions that come under federal jurisdiction. He pointed out very clearly his reliance on the auditor's reports.
Now for a whole new creature that is being created in this legislation, we are going to tell him that he will have to do with one auditor's report.
Even in the world of medicine they recognize that a second opinion is also very important for a patient. You go to the doctor, he examines you and says: "Well, it is your liver. If you want a second opinion, it is your kidney."
People have availability to second opinions. I see the member for Mississauga South shaking his head. The dual audit system for the banks has served Canadians well. What we are creating here is the potential for very large and complex financial institutions. Yet we are suggesting and saying to them that you only need one auditor.

My hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands is sitting there agreeing with me most vociferously, and I appreciate that very much.
In carrying on I want to talk about the bill which is before us which amends the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act to extend the February 1990 budget's per capita freeze on EPF transfers for a further three years to 1994-95.
However, it has no effect on transfers in the current fiscal year or the next. EPF transfers will continue to grow with population increases in each province. This is the largest single transfer program that the federal government has. It transfers $20 billion in 1991-92 to the provinces. It is provided to all provinces on an equal per capita basis and increases annually with each province's population.
Historically these transfers were made to help the provinces in the area of health care and post-secondary education. However, provinces are able to use these transfers according to their own priorities. That was a decision that was made, as hon. members pointed out today back, I believe, in 1977.
There are a great number of university presidents. There are a great number of those in the health care system who accuse the provinces of not in fact applying the money to those areas for which they were intended. If we go back to that type of thing, I am sure that will be one of the things that will be studied between the provinces and the federal government.
There, of course, has to be an accounting system, a check, and so on and so forth on that type of thing. I believe that when it was changed in 1977 it was done for a very good reason. Because they are examining the transfers, the methods of transfers, tax points versus cash, et cetera, that will be one of the things that will be looked at.
Government Orders
To the critics of the extension of the EPF freeze I want to say this, Mr. Speaker. For decades the Government of Canada has provided large and growing financial support to the provinces. As a matter of fact, while deficits were going up federally some of the provincial governments were balancing out their budgets on what they received from the federal government. I think that is fair to say.
Almost $37 billion in federal transfers are now simply too large to exempt from our expenditure restraint program. If 25 per cent or 30 per cent of your budget is going to the provinces in the form of these transfer payments then they are part of the expense problem of the federal government.
If in fact they are part of the problem, then they have to be part of the solution. I think that goes without saying.
In working to get down our deficit, we have to control these transfers to the provinces in a realistic way. So the transfers are affected. I think many people would agree with that.
I listened to my colleagues from the NDP again today complaining that medicare money was going to fix roads, and for uses by provincial governments other than for what they were intended. That was the claim made today. I have heard that many times from people across this country who are concerned about transfers to the provinces.
If that is the case and if the federal government has to rein in its expenditures, if the Canadian people, the constituents in Brampton, the constituents in Don Mills, the constituents that I meet everywhere, are saying that we have to cut back on expenditures and 30 per cent of expenditures are transfers to the provinces, then they must participate.
At the same time the provinces should cut back on their expenditures as well. They have many areas where they can cut back which would not detrimentally affect medicare or would not detrimentally affect post-secondary education.
They too have a responsibility for trimming the fat from their operations. To give provinces credit, I believe that in the last couple of years most of the provincial governments have realized that and have done that. They have made some tough decisions as well and have started to cut back.

December 2, 1991
Government Orders
I am concerned about my province of Ontario. I am very concerned about the way it is increasing deficit spending and the problem it is in today. I am very concerned about that. While other provinces are toeing the line, it is giving huge pay increases. At a time when everybody else is toeing the line it is spending money in areas that are questionable. It could trim a lot of fat out of its government as well.
When all other provincial governments are going in one direction, the government of Ontario seems to be going in the opposite direction. I believe it is working at cross purposes for what is trying to be attempted right across this country. We are concerned about that.

and limousine industry regarding the increases mentioned have been considered. Everything possible has been done to accommodate these concerns.

Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity today to discuss the effect Bill C-20 has on one aspect only. That is the health care system of Canada.

Even if all financial constraints were lifted today, our health care system in Canada would still be in some difficulty.

Being poor in Canada does not deny you from being treated by a doctor or being admitted to any hospital. We can all be proud of the rigid standard of care to which most health professionals are committed.
In the last 30 years, provincially and federally, with a constantly expanding economy, governments mostly did not question the growth of the cost of the medical care system. Today we find this experience of the last 30 years can no longer continue. This government and every province are faced with increasing deficits. The deficit of this government continues to be in the neighbourhood of
$30 billion. Our national debt now far exceeds $400 billion.
Thirty-seven cents of every tax dollar collected in Canada today does not pay for one doctor's visit, does not pay for one medical procedure; 37 cents does not pay for one drug administered, does not pay for one hour of nursing care or does not pay for the use of one hospital bed. Out of every dollar collected, 37 cents goes to pay the interest on the national debt. That means we have 63 cents remaining to administer to the affairs of this total country. Health care, as we all know, takes a substantial amount of the balance.
What I am trying to get at is what we have to do and what this government must do to try and find a new way. That is where this government has failed. We must begin to restructure our health care system and this again is where this government has failed. We must develop a comprehensive national strategy and again this government has failed to do that.
A government cannot unilaterally cut health care costs in this country, as it is trying to do with the legislation that is before this House today. A federal government must take the lead with its counterparts in the provinces and the municipalities to bring into line and to bring into focus the competing bureaucracies, federally, provincially and municipally, all that are involved in the health care system.
A good federal government must take the lead to define what a health care system truly is. Remove those social programs that have become a financial albatross around the necks of the health delivery system and we should take health related matters right out of the health budget so that we can truly define what it is.
A good federal government must take the lead to be rigorous in assessment, to prove the value of new technologies, to prove the value of expensive drugs and other costly health procedures.
A federal government must take the lead to monitor carefully treatments that may be done in homes of Canadians or clinics rather than the use of expensive hospital beds.
A federal government must take the lead to establish systems that monitor Canadians who have preventable diseases so that they can find out what these diseases
December 4, 1991

are. They can no longer be ignored until they reach the expensive crisis stage for treatment.

A federal government must take the lead to renew the health system from within, using those invaluable human resources we already have within our health care system.
A federal government must lead the way in all these important areas, working in close co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities, all which are already involved in the very important health care field. Private Members' Business

Analysis of the data revealed that many students are engaging in high risk sexual behaviour, despite being quite knowledgeable about safe sexual practices. Madam Speaker, I would like to advise the member for South West Nova that the government does not have a high interest rate policy. It is quite the opposite. The policy is geared to achieving durable lower interest rates through reducing inflation, as she probably knows.
Our policy we believe is working. As inflation pressures have eased in recent months, interest rates have declined in step. Short-term interest rates are more than 625 basis points lower than at their peak last May. Interest rate declines will continue and they will be sustainable.
Let me turn now to the exchange rate which she speaks of. There is no target or target range for the dollar. The exchange rate is determined by market forces. I think the member knows that but is just causing a bit of mischief.
The relative value of our dollar is affected by many factors, not just interest rates, such as inflation performance and prospects, investor confidence in the economy, international and political and economic uncertainty and the borrowing practices of Canadian businesses and governments. These can all affect the dollar.
It is clear that the Canadian interest rates are no reason for the increase in the exchange rate over the last year or so. Provincial government borrowings and international uncertainty are contributing to the dollar. They played key roles in the value of the dollar. Provincial governments placed $10.9 billion in new debt issues in the foreign financial markets in the first half of this year. This is double the amount that was placed in all of 1990.

Political uncertainty also affects the dollar. The problems in the Soviet Union, the Middle East and elsewhere have meant increased demand for safe haven currencies. This has produced a shift by the European and Asian investors into the North American market.
While the exchange rate does affect our competitiveness, the root cause of the deterioration in our competitiveness, is the more rapid increase in wage costs and the slower increase in productivity in Canada than in our major trading partners.

Establishing a heritage day in Canada is not a new idea but it is a very worth-while idea. Here we are, one of the most privileged people in the world living in one of the greatest countries in the world and we have unity problems. We seem to stress the negative. The fact of the matter is that unlike our friends south of the border, the Americans, we do not celebrate enough. We do not flaunt our successes enough. We do not show our pride enough. The Americans perhaps go too far because they show their pride and wear their pride on their lapels or on their sleeves. We tend to be shy and diffident. While I would not suggest that we should be just like the Americans, I think we do have to tell the Canadian story because it is a wonderful stoiy.
Unlike America, this country was not bom in revolution. We have a peaceful history. We have had peaceful evolution. We should have great pride in that. We should be very proud. We tend, however, to sit back and be quite defensive about this country. We do not have to be defensive at all. Let us go on the offensive and tell the world how great we are.
I can think of so many things to celebrate. We are coming up to our 125th birthday of Confederation and what a good time it would be to establish a national heritage day. Think of the private sector-public sector partnership we have had in this country. We have had a tremendous partnership. It is one of the reasons for the success of this country. We have not done it just on private moneys or private initiative. We have had a

wonderful and very productive partnership involving government and the private sector.

Medicare, established in the 1960s, is still one of the great public health models and is envied, I would think, in most parts of the world. Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood for his remarks with respect to how we can assist this country in putting forward a system for our infrastructure, particularly in transportation. I also thank him very much for his kind words about the work in transportation that I have done.
Let me answer my friend by saying that what Canada lacks is a national transportation policy that would extend all modes of transportation: rail, water, air and roads into an infrastructure that would cause this economy to come back to what it once was.
Let me talk for a moment about the roadway system. In my particular area, VIA Rail has been cancelled from Sudbury right through to Winnipeg. As a result, we do not have any passenger rail service, which is so vital to any area of this country, but particularly in northern Ontario. With the absence of passenger rail service on days like today when the planes are not flying, we only have one means of transportation, roads. It is with trucks and cars that people move back and forth in all of the communities in that particular area and I am sure it is synonymous with every other area in Canada.
What we find now, Mr. Speaker, is that the infrastructure of our roadway system is deteriorating to a point where we have more accidents on our roads than we have ever experienced before. This is due primarily to the fact that the roads are not maintained as well as they once were. Coupled with the fact that the roadways are taking the excess transportation that should have been going on railways, it means that we have huge trucks on the roads. We have an economy that is resource based and we have logging trucks and so on.

February 4, 1992
Government Orders
We do not have the will through either the provincial government, although it promised that all kinds of great things were going to happen in the north, or this government which does not have the resources to provide for all of those communities in northern Ontario and other areas of Canada to spend on the infrastructure that is so vitally needed.
I just heard from my friends on the side here, Mr. Speaker, that they spent a fortune on northern Ontario. Let me say unequivocally and without fear of contradiction that all we have heard in northern Ontario is words and the promises that are made. We get ministers there making all kinds of promises and it has not, like other governments before it, followed through. That is a dilemma that all people in northern Ontario are facing, the dilemma that governments promise things that they cannot deliver. That is what is happening in Ontario, and we see it happening on the other side of the House.
Getting back to the point of my colleague on transportation needs, we need rail transport, additional roads and more access to the air systems of Canada. Thank you very much for asking that question.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my place today to respond to the motion from the hon. member for Davenport.
It was recommended that the government establish a royal commission on the pricing practices of the pharmaceutical industry.
I know that the hon. member is motivated by a genuine concern for the impact the drug prices have on consumers, and I know that he is concerned about the ability of provincial governments to respond to increasing prices.
February 10, 1992

As much as we can acknowledge the undoubted good intentions of this motion, I am afraid that the motion for a royal commission is misplaced.
Any royal commission, as we know, imposes a large expense on the public treasury. Clearly there are important issues which must be examined by commissions of inquiry, but if we are going to burden the taxpayer with the expense, first we had better make sure that we genuinely do need a commission.
I am afraid that when one looks at the proposal and at the state of the pharmaceutical industry in general, I cannot see that we should inflict upon taxpayers the cost of this kind of study.
To begin with, several items the hon. member would like to examine fall under provincial jurisdiction. I am sure that it was not the intention of the hon. member for Davenport to intrude on provincial responsibilities for pharmaceutical price controls at the retail level, but that is the effect of his motion.
In fact, hon. members are well aware that the provinces have demonstrated a great concern for drug pricing. The challenges vary from province to province.
Each province is more capable of focusing on its own needs than a federal inquiry would be. In fact, some provinces have recognized their own responsibility to investigate these matters.
Both Ontario and British Columbia have already conducted their own commissions into the areas that fall under their jurisdiction. I am certain that no one in this House would endorse a commission that would only duplicate that work.
Any federal inquiry would inevitably get bogged down into the complexities of provincial systems over which this House has no jurisdiction whatsoever.
The issue of provincial responsibilities brings me to another reason why I believe this House should vote against this motion.
Hon. members from both sides are no doubt aware that the minister of health and welfare is committed to working with the provinces to ensure reasonably priced drugs for Canadians. In fact, the minister met with his provincial counterparts on January 27 to discuss this matter and other issues of mutual concern.
Private Members' Business
I am reassured by the commitment of the Minister of National Health and Welfare that prices will be kept reasonable for consumers, and I am encouraged by his efforts to work with the provinces on the issue.
At the federal level, we have the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board. Since the Patent Act was amended in 1987, the board, regardless of any limits on its mandate, has kept price increases for patented drugs below the increase in the Consumer Price Index. The board will be given enhanced powers to keep prices of patented drugs reasonable.
At the same time that this government is working with the provinces to ensure reasonable drug prices, it is working to encourage more research and development in the Canadian pharmaceutical industry.
There have already been some remarkable results. Glaxo Canada, one of the largest research-based pharmaceutical companies in Canada announced on January 16 that it was moving ahead with plans to build a $70 million manufacturing plant in Mississauga.

Mr. Speaker, my speech this morning will be relatively brief.
Public Service 2000 is indeed an excellent initiative and will certainly prove worthwhile for all Canadians. All members of this House have great respect for Public Service employees. We need them, and we realize that they are doing an excellent job.
I do not think it is in any way disparaging to Public Service employees if we look for ways to improve efficiency and renew a public service which seems to have been operating on the same principles for the past 25 years.
In my speech this morning I want to express my support for Bill C-26, and I will explain why. Public Service 2000 will achieve the following objectives: Initially, change internal management rules to make them more flexible, more effective and more service oriented. Throughout this initiative, we see there is a very real respect for all public service employees. Our purpose is simply to make certain adjustments to the technological developments that have taken place during the past 25 years, to change the rules and make it easier for the public servant to do the job he has to do as part of his duties.
It is clear that the Public Service must concentrate on providing better service to all Canadians. This also means updating the rules on collective bargaining, staffing and human resource management. The reform will be prepared by a task force created in January 1991, which will be responsible for simplifying the position classification system by abolishing occupational categories, reducing the number of occupational groups from 71 to 23, and simplifying classification standards and reducing the number of classification levels.
I repeat this will make the Public Service far more responsive to all its employees and help it to continue improving services to the public.

Despite all these changes, many groups will continue to exist, such as specialists and technical jobs, but the administrative sector will be consolidated in a single occupational group to be known as general services.

Of that, $2.2 billion went to dairy farmers. That was a concocted figure. The actual figure was $267 billion to the industrial milk producers of Canada. The fluid milk producers got nothing. Look at the difference between the industry in Canada, a healthy, vibrant industry that supplies the Canadian consumer with ample quantities of excellent products at reasonable prices, and the system of utter chaos in the United States, where literally thousands upon thousands of dairy farmers are being forced out of business.

Rather they hand out another $790,000 to the Canadian Consumers' Association to attack the best marketing systems in the world that have served us so well.
I have to ask the minister why he is not taking the lead to correct these erroneous statements. Why does he not defend his producers at home here in Canada? Is he using the same laid back tactics in defence of our marketing board systems at GATT?

consumer, an increase of 97 per cent; cheese showed a very moderate increase to the producer and the manufacturer, but at the retail level an increase of 86 per cent. Mr. Speaker, the government would like to use the opportunity following several weeks of media claims and statements in the House to bring hon. members up to date on the department's actions concerning silicone gel-filled breast implants.
First, let me say that Health and Welfare is very concerned about the comments expressed over the fear of cancer following breast implant surgery. Let me put a stop to speculations right now. Dr. Hans Berkel and his colleagues in Alberta demonstrated clearly that women who have breast augmentation do not have an increased risk of breast cancer. He also found that breast implants do not decrease the survival of breast cancer patients.
This is a very powerful study. More than 11,000 breast implant patients were followed for an average of 10 years. Where 49 cases of breast cancer were expected in the normal population, 23 developed breast cancer after breast implants.
Rarely in the field of science can a better demonstration be made about the low risk of using a medical device. This work which was done in Canada by reputable epidemiologists is confirmed by a similar study done in the United States.

Adjournment Debate
I wish then to reassure the women in Canada who have silicone breast implants that at this time there is no evidence to support the scare tactics used by media and others.
Let us go on now to the basis of this whole discussion. This basis centres on the fact that the Department of National Health and Welfare makes its decisions on safety and effectiveness based on science, not on media reports, not on innuendo and not on testimony of unusual events.

The Constitution

I also had 20 speaking engagements at service clubs, schools and other interested organizations.
It was a very healthy process. It was a learning process not only for my constituents but for myself. I had a chance to hear them and get a sense of what they wanted from this country of ours.
To sum up, I am going to have to quote the Mexican ambassador to Canada. He says it best: "Canada is a success looking for a problem". Speech:
Madam Speaker, I wish that all Canadians could see the spectacle of the rat pack back at it.
I was talking about the requirements to ensure that Canadians can get jobs. One of the factors is to improve the efficiency of the labour market.
The first factor in improving our competitiveness is in improving the efficiency of our labour market through skills upgrading. On the other side of the House the other political parties recommend short-term, make-work solutions, but make-work projects are band-aid solutions.
As I said earlier, it may have been the favourite approach during the seventies to remedy what were cyclical labour market difficulties, but the evidence today to anyone who really cares about the problem and tries to explain why and understand why is overwhelming that in the face of major structural changes to the economy more than band-aid solutions are required to respond to the labour market needs of the 1990s.
The Canadian economy of today has increased skill requirements and the nature and type of work has changed. If we are to be internationally competitive, we must respond appropriately to these changes through training. Make work is not the solution. We have structural problems, not cyclical problems.
Yesterday Speaker, I was meeting with the council of automotive and repair people and one garage owner here in Ottawa was telling me that he had put ads in the paper trying to get a qualified mechanic for his garage here in Ottawa and he could not find anyone qualified.
There is a shortage in Canada of skilled workers. Unemployed people have to tap these opportunities of training and retraining in order to get better qualifications in order to get into the jobs. In the long run training has benefits for both individuals and the country. We should consider that by the year 2000, and that is not far away, almost two-thirds of all new jobs will require at
least one year of educational training beyond high school.
Back in the 1970s it was easy to get a job with just a grade 9 education, but that is no longer the reality today. That is not the case any more. Training is also good from a macro-economic perspective, because a highly skilled work force attracts foreign investment in Canada.
Training raises productivity. Workers with higher skills are employed in higher productivity jobs, earning higher wages and making Canada more competitive. For that reason the government's priority has been the development of a skilled work force to accommodate economic and social change. For the unemployed there is no better time to train than during forced periods of unemployment.
When the economy recovers, human capital is improved and workers are prepared to take an active role in the labour force. However, more could be done with available resources to improve labour market efficiency by shifting priorities from passive income assistance and transfer to active measures, and from social treatment of unemployment to a more economic one.
In the OECD study of active versus passive program expenditures, Canada ranked 20th out of 23 member countries with only 24 per cent. Only 24 per cent of Canada's labour market program expenditures was spent on active measures. We began the transition toward more active policies with the labour force development strategy in 1989.
It became evident over the years that passive income generated significant disincentives to seeking employment. It certainly did nothing to develop the skills of the unemployed to make them more employable and more productive members of the labour force.
I see you indicating that I should conclude my remarks, Madam Speaker. The hon. member and his party vehemently opposed in this House and in the Senate the changes to the UI program we introduced two years ago. From 1990 to 1992 we have tripled the $600 million spent to train unemployed Canadians. This has gone up. In 1992 we will be spend $1.8 billion to train unemployed Canadians. I think that speaks louder than the yapping of the hon. member.
February 14, 1992

Although the federal government supports education in a number of ways, since 1986 it has continually reduced its contributions to post-secondary education.

My friend for St. Boniface suggests that maybe it is $43 billion. Whatever it is, it is a very substantial figure. Those amounts are not subject to any spending restraints under this bill.
Government Orders
This is for restraint of government expenditures but it only applies to certain expenditures. The biggest single one is excluded. The government says it cannot take any responsibility for that, although the responsibility is direct and four-square. It rests clearly on the shoulders of the government. It is charged with managing the Canadian economy, not the opposition, and yet it says it cannot be responsible for that and will exclude it from the bill.
That is the first serious weakness in the bill. It indicates how silly and ridiculous it is for the government to bring forward this kind of legislation in this House. I am glad to see my colleague from Willowdale agrees.
The second aspect of this bill which is so silly is the lack of control on tax expenditures. Members may ask what tax expenditures are. The government may give a tax break to a group in order to induce some particular aspect of the Canadian economy. For example a special writeoff may be given on the development of a gold mine. Those operating the gold mine will not have to pay taxes during a certain development period, and obviously the government will forgo revenue. That is called a tax expenditure. The government gives up its right to tax the gold mine and bring in revenue it might otherwise get.
By introducing its budget the government says that it will give a preferential tax break to certain people in order to induce them to spend their money in a particular way.
It may give a child tax credit, for example, to those who have children to either encourage them to have children, or to assist them in paying the costs of looking after the children.
The tax break is a tax expenditure. It is giving away or forgoing revenue in order to achieve a desired result. This is all perfectly proper, but if you have a cap on expenditures, why would you not also cap tax expenditures?
Yet the government has left itself a free hand to spend the tax dollars that it does not actually bring in. It is saying in this bill that it will limit the amount of tax dollars it spends on everything except the public debt, but will not in any way restrict its right to forgo tax dollars and not bring them into the pot.

February 18, 1992
Government Orders
In other words, give tax breaks to its wealthy friends, the Tory fat cats. They are the same people who got the tax break when this government took office and have been getting them all along ever since. That is what the government is proposing to do. It is saying it is not going to be hamstrung in any way by legislation in the House of Commons that restricts its ability to give those tax breaks, in other words to make tax expenditures.
If the government was serious about controlling government expenditures, surely it would deal with that issue in a straightforward and responsible way and include that in the bill. It has chosen not to do so.
The third argument against this silly legislation, this ridiculous bill, was made by the minister himself. The poor minister stood there, and really he must have been very embarrassed to have to introduce this kind of legislation in the House.
Yet his argument was that if any government wants to change this in future, when it introduces its budget making the change, it will have to introduce an amendment to this act as well. Imagine, what could be simpler?
If you do not like the restrictions in the bill, you introduce your budget proposing higher expenditures and in the budget you announce there will be changes to this bill. It happens every day in every budget.
The government announces that there will be tax changes. It announces the tax changes in the budget and then it introduces a bill to amend the Income Tax Act. That is all it is going to do with this bill. It is exactly the same thing.
This is nothing but a scam as the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood so ably says. This is ridiculous. It is silly and it should not be allowed.
The ministers of the Crown who have an obligation to be here and participate in debate absent themselves from this Chamber when government bills are under discussion. It is a national disgrace.
If they are going to bring in silly bills like this, the least they can do is sit here and listen to the debate. They choose to absent themselves in their entirety, 39 of them. It is wrong. They have an obligation as members of this House to sit here when government legislation is under consideration.
If they are going to propose something so stupid, the least they can do is listen to the debate.

Some countries undertake military or bold action in order to make themselves more popular in the polls when they are suffering electorally. In this particular case, the government has targeted a number of groups. One of them, I maintain, is the civil service. I really find this very, very unfortunate.

Obviously we cannot manage and govern as we did a number of years ago. Obviously we need to change the rules and regulations. Obviously we need to find that right balance between permitting the managers to undertake a number of decisions within their discretion. At the same time we need to protect employees and the rights they have acquired overtime.

February 21, 1992
Government Orders

We need that balance between managers and employees who have acquired certain rights through years of collective bargaining, and I think the two can be combined without denying employees their rights. It would be unfortunate if we were to do that.

As you know, this particular piece of legislation will permit people to hire, fire and transfer employees without the normal protections they now have. The merit principle is in jeopardy. There will be contracting out. I find it interesting that the government claims that contracting out saves money. When I asked on the Order Paper for a record of everything that had been contracted out, I was told that under a certain figure, the figures are not available. Why? What in the world are we trying to hide?
If you are really saving money, you ought to be proud, government, to show it in black and white. Of course the suspicion is that there is no money being saved. These are simply ways in order to permit those who are friendly to government to profit from government. Until I receive a clear, precise answer to the question I have raised, I shall continue to doubt the government's intentions in this particular matter.
I believe I could find a great deal of support for my feeling that there has been inadequate consultation with a number of people. The government will cite the meetings, but ask the employees whether or not they feel comfortable. Ask the employees whether or not there needs to be additional discussions. There does need to be additional discussions. This is major legislation that will affect services throughout Canada.

Another example of a government that is undermining the very foundations of this country is that it has launched attacks on VIA Rail, Air Canada, Canada Post-all institutions that bound this country together, that made it strong and far more united than it is today. March 9, 1992

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just spoke, spoke very well of some of the problems that attend the life of being a member of Parliament and attend the issues which this bill, in some respects, raises. I say in some respects because what is wrong with the bill is that it does attempt to deal with one particular problem in principle in isolation from the rest of the package, if you like, of issues which the hon. member who just spoke raised and that is the whole matter of compensation for members of Parliament and everything that involves.
Therefore, I would support, rather than this bill, the call by the hon. member who just spoke and the call by others over the years, that in some way or another these questions be taken out of our hands. We cannot win in terms of public opinion no matter what we do, as long as the public continue to be cynical about the political process. I might add that the public have always been to a degree cynical about politicians and the political process. In that sense we do not live in some new age.
I remember going through a book that had been prepared Fifty Years of Headlines. One of the headlines I noticed in the year 1906 was about MPs raising their salaries to an exorbitant rate. So as long ago as 1906 the media and, presumably others, were enjoying making members of Parliament out to look bad.
I think this has been an industry for a long time. No doubt, sometimes we have collectively deserved that criticism and other times we have not.
I was disturbed to hear the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood get up and say that we are the most distrusted people in the country. Frankly I do not feel that way. I do not feel like I am one of the most distrusted people in the country. I am still proud to be a member of Parliament. I still feel good about being a member of Parliament. If the member for Broadview-Greenwood feels like one of the most distrusted people in the country, I feel sorry for him. Sure people are critical of politicians and they are critical of the political process. But I think that is an exaggeration.
What we have here in the form of this bill and in the form of the comments made by the member for Broadview-Greenwood and other comments that have been made from time to time around this place is a form of piety, of piousness, of self-congratulatory heroism at the expense of one's colleagues.
The principle that the member opposite wants to promote, that all money should be treated the same, is a principle that I do not think anybody in my party would have any difficulty with. I think it is a principle we have promoted in the past and continue to promote.
All we are saying about this bill is that by itself it cannot deal with the over-all problem, both with respect to perception and with respect to reality as it pertains to members of Parliament compensation package.
March 12, 1992

The member is dreaming in technicolour if he thinks that if our expense allowance was to be made taxable and we then found it to be inadequate that we could just simply stroll back in here and increase it so that we would be getting exactly the same amount without bringing down upon ourselves much more criticism than the criticism he feels he is responding to now, I think he is being quite unrealistic.
Therefore, I go back to my original point, that no matter how we deal with it, what we need to do is somehow get it out of our hands. That point was made by my leader the other day with respect to the whole issue of MPs pensions, which has become such an issue, that is to get it out of our hands, to have somebody else make that judgment and probably to go beyond what we have done over the years, which is by law to have two retired MPs look at it. People could still say: "Well it is still part of the club". Let us have a mixture of people look at it and come in with some recommendations. I venture to suggest that if we did our jobs here, the responsibilities that we have might be judged by these outsiders to be worthy of more compensation than we receive now. I do not know.
The problem is that it might be the case in spite of everything everybody believes, that the greatest restraint on MPs salaries and other things is to some degree the fact that we do have to set them ourselves and we are politically answerable for that. Maybe there have been times when that has not been the case. I am certainly open to that, having voted against an increase myself in 1981, the last time there was an increase.
But it may be the case that the very fact we are in control of it actually acts as a restraint. It may be hard to believe, given everything people say these days about our benefits, et cetera. It will not be just us who will have to take our chances with whatever those people will recommend, the public will have to take its chances with what an independent review of our situation might recommend. We will all have to take our chances.

And the GATT, as my colleague says. Not only would the resolution ensure a trade war with the United States, it would tell Canada and by implication our Latin American trading partners that we are not prepared to work with them, that we are no longer interested in creating a trading future based on a framework of stable and orderly rules. Make no mistake, that is what the NAFTA negotiations are all about and that is what we would turn our back on.
The GATT world trade talks are an integral and critical element in Canada's trade strategy. It is neither an alternative to nor unrelated to the FTA or the NAFTA. They are all a concerted effort by Canada and its trading partners to create a more ordered and more predictable global trading system. Each is an effort to strengthen the rules, to improve procedures to resolve disputes and to bind nations to a common approach to the regulation of trade and investment.

For Canada, the success of these negotiations is critically important. It will help us gain and defend access to the markets of the world, including the United States and Mexico. In other words, we have not placed our eggs in a single basket, rather we are defending and promoting Canadian trade interests wherever there is an opportunity to do so.
I just came back from an OECD meeting of science and technology ministers having to do with the economy and growth. The whole meeting, with governments of every stripe, concentrated on how we can all be more prosperous, how we can all trade with each other, how we can all have economies of benefit if we have the rules of the game clearly spelled out. That is what this is all about.
Our trade with the United States is important, but so is our trade with the rest of the world.
In 1991, our trade with all of our trading partners totalled $381.6 billion; that is one-quarter of our Gross Domestic Product. Trade with countries other than the United States totalled $124.7 billion. You have to remember that merchandise exports of $34.1 billion translate into more than a million jobs for Canadians. Our merchandise trade with countries other than the United States is growing. Our global approach has been instrumental in a 5 per cent annual growth in that trade since we took office.
Those numbers are the result of Canada's multi-faceted, global trade strategy. Canadian entrepreneurs know that wherever they go they can count on the support of Canada's 1,060 trade commissioners. They know where to find them at 90 offices across the world, at headquarters and at international trade centres across Canada. They know they can rely on hundreds of agreements that Canada has negotiated to smooth their way: air agreements, double tax agreements, economic co-operation agreements, investment agreements, export financing agreements.
Canadian exporters know that they can draw on the support programs developed to assist their marketing efforts: the Program for Export Market Development (PEMD), trade fairs and missions, the Strategic Ventures Program, Going Global, CIDA Inc., the EDC and more.

Speech:
The warming is chilling. I do not intend to make a pun or make fun of that. This is a deadly serious mattef.
What may lie ahead for us is a very different world than what we were used to. That is why I say the environment is the most important issue.
I look, as do all of us, at the letters I get from my riding. We now get faxes and telephone calls. They are very interesting, at least in my case. I note when environmental matters come up that they are inevitably from young people. When we talk to young people in they schools they ask us about the environment. I remember talking to students in the Coquitlam and Port Moody schools in my riding, a suburb of Vancouver with excellent schools and students who are very motivated in environmental concerns. Inevitably the question is the environment.
I was thinking today about the upcoming election. Someone mentioned that it may be within a year. I remember an all-party debate at Centennial High School in Coquitlam, British Columbia, during the last election. The teachers did a bit of a poll as to which party's candidate was winning. I must say that I was somewhat shocked because I was in third place in that poll as we went in.
I remember we only had a short period of time, a few minutes, and I chose to comment on the environment. When I came out of the debate I was quite far ahead in the poll because clearly I had chosen an issue the students were really interested in. They wanted to vote for someone who would champion such issues.
I took part in the study of the previous bill on the environment in the last Parliament. I was on the legislative committee. Having had that experience, I want to congratulate the members who took part in this legislative committee, especially the member for The Battle-fords-Meadowlake. When he goes back to speak to the high school students in his riding in Saskatchewan I hope he will say: "I took part in the process that led to Bill C-13" because it is really important.
I say to the hon. member who is behind me in the House that I took part earlier this year in a bill on gun control. It took a long time and a lot of effort. I remember thinking at the time: You do not get a lot of credit for this; you do not get your name in the headlines on this. There is a lot of work behind the scenes. It is a heck of a lot of work and I want to congratulate him.
The world may not know what he is doing, but young people will know and are concerned about what he is doing. As a matter of fact, I noticed that the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake has spoken on this issue a number of times. I was just trying to find copies of his speech. I just want to quote the hon. member when he said: "Our children are inheriting a country which is sick and diseased compared to the state of our country a generation ago. Our ozone layer has been destroyed to the extent where the federal Minister of the Environment has warned that our children should not expose themselves to the sun. Many of our lakes and rivers are dead and dying. Our forests are sold off in unimaginably large tracts to pulp and paper companies. We continue to encourage global warming and our children have been robbed of the opportunity to share our environment with many species of animals, plants, fish and birds now extinct through bad choices we have made as individuals and through our government. We can change the future".
I hope this bill will go some way to changing that future because the environment is our future. Canada must have the best environment in the world, and that is what we should be committed to as politicians. I hope this bill will go some way to doing that.
I just want to go over a couple of parts in the bill and make some comments on them. The bill, as I understand it, sets out to trigger the set-off of environmental assessment. We have seen a number of projects such as the Rafferty-Alameda project in Saskatchewan, the James Bay project in Quebec, the Oldman Dam project in Alberta and the Kemano project in British Columbia. The bill triggers these environment assessments. The intensity of the assessment from a simple screening to a full panel or mediation is dealt with; what sort of projects, activities or undertakings are to be assessed; the factors to be assessed are taken into account; who is to do the assessing; the role of the public; and the responsibility and authority of the minister.
Now it is very important that these assessments be clear and we set out a procedure. We in the New Democratic Party would like to see a better environmental assessment procedure. We believe the assessment should be done by an independent agency free from political pressure or influence peddling and the decision should be final and binding.
March 16, 1992

I am going to conclude there and come back later in the debate to speak about the role of the environmental community which was involved in this bill, and I applaud that, and some of the shortcomings of the bill which still treats environment and economic development as tradeoffs. I want to talk about where I think we can strengthen the bill by making a much clearer process, a stronger process and better public input.
Let me conclude where I began. As the hon. member from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake has said, I have visited his riding and it is a beautiful environment.
I want to conclude by saying that the environment is the major issue for the future. The young people of Canada understand that. They demand that their members of Parliament, as far as possible, put partisanship aside, as has been done a lot in this committee, to strengthen this bill, to make a strong environmental bill with clear protections and a clear process when we are to begin big projects in this country which could damage our environment. We have just begun the fight.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, as we have heard in the speeches today in this House, the complexity of this bill is becoming clear. There are major motions still being put forward at the report stage of this bill.
I would like to focus on Motion No. 26 in particular. The language in it is: "before irrevocable decisions are made". It is very clear from our most recent history on environmental concerns that we have the language in this legislation to ensure that environmental assessment carries through before irrevocable decisions are made. That means that, yes, things will have to slow down, that maybe development is not going to go at the pace the major corporations would want it to.
Canadians have told members of this House that there cannot be development without some consideration for the environment. We now know that the Supreme Court decision on the Oldman River has come down. This is not just a victory for the environmental movements, it is also a victory for the people who made it clear in the language of this motion that irrevocable decisions have been made. The Oldman River dam is now reportedly 25 storeys tall. The taxpayers of Alberta and the taxpayers of Canada will be the ones who are paying the bill on that. This is not responsible behaviour. It was pushed through with the assumption that all was going to be well and that provincial jurisdiction was going to be paramount.
The Supreme Court has decided: "No, wait a minute. There is federal paramountcy on environmental concerns". The Oldman River decision is crucial to the way we jig the kind of jurisdictional squabbles between the levels of government.
The federal government has to have supreme authority on environmental issues. It just makes good sense. Often in this House good sense does not prevail. Rivers do flow across provincial boundaries, air flows across not just provincial boundaries but international boundaries. My colleague from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake has pointed out that the environment does not respect the
March 16, 1992

nice little maps we have drawn on the globe. Therefore, we have to find the best way of determining how to care for the environment. Canada, that is the federal government, has to have the supreme authority on those decisions. Canada is the one that is speaking, not just for the country but for all the people in each of the territories and the provinces.
Motion No. 26 makes certain that the environment has to be considered before irrevocable decisions are made, so that the tax dollars that went into that 25 storey structure on the Oldman River will not be wasted in the future. It is not irresponsible environmentalists that are trying to block progress, it is very responsible environmentalists wanting to ensure that the project will only proceed when all things have been considered. That is the complexity of this bill and we will be talking about it over the next few days. For those people who are watching, please bear with us. It is complex and we want to do the best we can for environmental assessment in Canada because it is so important.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the member for Skeena, our environment critic, spoke eloquently on this amendment to clause 17. The amendment is in the name of my friend from Davenport who is a former environment minister and whose amendments and remarks are always worth considering and are usually persuasive in this House. I rise to speak on that.
The hon. member for Skeena mentioned the notion of Williston Lake. I happened to be with him one time going up that lake. It is really quite startling. It is a 100-mile long lake that was created by us, really, by engineers and so on. They created that lake and that caused some very strange things to happen.
The member mentioned what it was like in winter and the illusion of the ice, the illusion of normality. One should see it in summer. There used to be some beautiful native villages and a beautiful valley there.
It was decided that we needed this power. There was no environmental assessment, nothing. There was a dam. The Bennett dam was built there. In the summer you cannot go along that lake in a canoe because, if you do, you are liable to get a missile hitting you from the bottom. The trees at the bottom were left there when it was flooded. Over time they have become loose. As you go along, occasionally the trees will just come up like a guided missile from the bottom and surface on the lake. People have actually been hurt in boats and canoes. They cannot go on the lake.
It is important that we now get a modem environmental process that really works. That is why the minister's discretion must be looked at very carefully. As the member for Skeena said, there must be enforceable national standards. We must not set up an act in which a weak minister or a weak government like this Conservative government can start ignoring things to help their
friends as they did with the Oldman Dam in Saskatchewan.
I know we are going into Question Period, so we will come back to this amendment. I hope the House can support this amendment so that we can make a strong, enforceable standard here.

Madam Speaker, my remarks will be very brief. I want to compliment the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment and all committee members on this work.
I would like to put forward to members that there is confusion from time to time in the overlapping jurisdictions. I want to bring this down to my own community in Toronto where we have three rivers that flow through the centre of our city; the Don River, the Rouge River and the Humber River. They flow into Lake Ontario which is a lake that we share with the United States. These are the most polluted rivers in all of Canada.
For years we have had the toxic and biological waste from the largest city in Canada flowing down these rivers into Lake Ontario. They are now just chemical cauldrons.
It seems that because of the overlapping jurisdictions from the municipality to the province, to the conservation boards and ultimately, because of the Great Lakes, the federal jurisdiction, there is always the pointing of fingers at each other, that the municipality is responsible for a certain facet and then ultimately the province. action plan or the resources to begin reclaiming these rivers.

The Algonguins of Barrier Lake could not get the support of the province to stop the clear-cutting. It was a clear cut case where the province should have stepped in and stopped it.
Yet, we as a national government, other than moral suasion, were not really in a position to do anything about it. We have a similar situation in Alberta with the pulp and paper mills going into the Athabasca River region.
My concern is that there should be some clear definition so that the national government can step in and put a much more aggressive position forward, the ultimate position when the operating authorities fail to act.
I hope in committee that specific examples like that can be addressed. We, as a national government, seem to have either relinquished or do not have that final thrust.
I hope that we can have a clear-cut definition of our responsibility by the time we bring this bill to its final resting place.
