Madam Speaker, as has been said at report stage, the environmental assessment bill before us today is the single most important piece of environmental legislation ever to face this country.
The bill represents a significant step forward from the existing environmental assessment legislation under EARP. It reflects a great number of changes presented not only by myself and my New Democratic colleagues but also members of the environmental community as well.
The bill is not perfect. We said that at report stage. It is not the bill that we would write if we were on the other side of the House. It is not the bill that I would write if I were the Minister of the Environment, and it is not the bill that I would expect if my colleague from Skeena were the Minister of the Environment in a New Democratic Party government.
Some of the problems with it are not known and will only be discovered through years of working with the new law.

March 17, 1992
Government Orders
The government's acceptance of my suggestion for a five-year review or at least the pieces of the proposal that I put together for a five-year review go a long way to ensuring that in the future some of the unforeseen problems can be addressed. Some of the problems are obvious even now, and I hope to have the time today to mention some of them.
My New Democratic Party colleagues and I are committed to improving this act and the process it outlines for environmental assessment.
The bill still tends to reinforce the primacy of development over the environment, and thus reinforces the old trade-off between development and the environment, a trade-off under which the level of environmental destruction demands that we do away with it.
Environmental legislation in Canada should be far-reaching and ensure that environmental considerations are accorded the importance they deserve. Bill C-13, even with all its improvements, still comes up short in this regard.
Let us outline the elements of the legislation dealing with environmental assessment as to what they should include. What are the ingredients to developing an environmental assessment process that will truly aim at preserving and enhancing the environment for our children?
It must be reviewed by an independent agency, resulting in a final and binding decision. It must contain a broad definition of environment and must apply universally to a variety of initiatives, including government policy making.
Discretionary decision-making within the assessment process must be minimized and the accountability of those decision makers must be ensured. Proponents of undertakings must demonstrate that the purpose of the project is justified and that there is an environmentally acceptable need for the undertaking.
Proponents should prove that their undertaking is better than alternatives to their proposal in terms of environmental protection. There should be a significant public role early and often in the planning process and thus must contain provisions relating to public notice and comments, access to information and participant funding.
The final decision must be implementable, enforceable and subject to terms and conditions where necessary. Future monitoring of the environmental impact of projects, especially when combined with other projects and activities, must be accounted for.
The government, in response to pressure I believe from our side of the House and many representatives in the environmental movement, did respond to amendments which moved us closer to environmental assessment legislation which incorporates many of these needs. Others were fudged and some were ignored completely.
Yesterday and earlier today during report stage discussion, the government had the opportunity to respond to the right of Canadians to a safe and healthy environment. It could have accepted amendments which would have allowed for regulations to be reviewed by this House. It could have adopted an amendment which would have insured that this piece of environmental assessment legislation was thoroughly reviewed every five years and not just once five years hence.
In fact, during committee discussion, the minister and other government members said time and time again how important the regulations are to this bill. Yet when it came time for public scrutiny, it decided that it could not happen.
The government often mentions that this bill deals with a very new process and we will not know many of its weaknesses until it is put into practice. The acceptance by this government of an amendment calling for a five-year review does go a long way to putting a mechanism in place to address many of the weaknesses.
While environmental assessment needs to be enshrined in federal legislation, there remains a weakness right at the beginning of the bill. The government refused to include wording in the preamble of the bill which would have reflected the constitutional authority of the act. Including a peace, order and good government clause would have given the bill the stature it is due, providing certainty as to the constitutional basis of the act.
Unfortunately, this omission may open the door for more and more court challenges on behalf of provinces trying to attract industry and sacrifice the environment in the process. The Canadian Environmental Law Association states: "The failure to do so causes us to question the government's profane commitment to achieving a

new and meaningful environmental assessment program for Canada."

Private Members' Business
five years. Perhaps if we did not have elections more than once a decade we could save a lot more money. If we did not have elections at all think of the money we could save.

In reply to a question I raised in the House on February 28, the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship said that even in these times of constitutional crisis, that program had to be abolished because, and I quote: "After hundreds of cases one would imagine that we now have that base of jurisprudence".

March 19, 1992
Adjournment Debate
In reply to other questions raised on that same day, the minister stated that the program should be supported by other groups, maybe at the provincial level, or by non-governmental organizations. Let us examine the three cases, the three issues.
First of all, he mentioned that there was enough jurisprudence. The financial support that was given led to major decisions by the Supreme Court of Canada. The jurisprudence is far from being complete. The witnesses that appeared before the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons on March 10th, 1992 pointed to that. The director of the Court Challenges Program, among others, said: "The courts have so far had very few opportunities to interpret sections 16 to 20 of the charter concerning services offered in both official languages by the governments of Canada and New Brunswick". She also said: "Because of the inherent slowness of the judicial process and of dilatory procedures often used by federal and provincial governments, the vast majority of test cases brought up by special interest groups representing women, disabled persons and minorities, as well as by other groups likely to benefit from the support given by the program, are still before the trial courts or a court of appeal". She also added that no court had yet ruled on the implementation of the language equality rights provided in section 15 of the charter.
Referring to the Mahe case now before the Supreme Court, Gerard Bertrand, chairman of the language rights committee, recognized that the implementation of section 23 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms would probably produce numerous court challenges in the years to come. Mr. Justice Dixon of the Supreme Court of Canada then replied: "It is impossible at this stage of development of section 23 to foresee all the circumstances pertaining to its enforcement."
Given these facts, it would seem unrealistic to conclude that the case law is sound and complete.

Let us take the Mahe case dealing with the educational rights provided for in section 23 of the charter and
involving the Alberta government. Let us take the Ford decision concerning the Brown shoes in Quebec dealing with the freedom of expression and the right to use languages other than French as regards public billposting which involves the province of Quebec. There is also the Forest case involving the province of Manitoba and judicial and legislative bilingualism. In 1978, again a province was challenged by a citizen.
To give provinces the responsibility of protecting minorities is somewhat the same as telling the Canadian people that we are going to put the fox in the hen house.
Now let us talk about the costs. The minister said that funds had to be cut. Well, the budget had been renewed in May 1990 at a cost of $13.75 million over five years. The expenditure would amount to $2.7 million. That is 10 cents per Canadian per year. This is not a big amount.
I plead with the Government. When the Constitution of our country is being scrutinized, the collective rights of Quebec, of native people and all the other groups and communities which will be before us should have a chance to be challenged in court.

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I move that the 23rd report of the Standing Committee on House Management, presented to the House on Friday, February 14, 1992, be concurred in.
It certainly is a pleasure for me to present and speak to this particular committee report. It has been an honour to take part in the debate and discussions relating to the experimental guidelines governing the broadcasting of committee meetings. That was a result of Standing Order 119.1(2).
I just want to quote a few things from the report because I think they are very important for all members here and certainly for the public.
On the one hand, there is the desire for openness of democratic political institutions and freedom of the press.
We can all understand and recognize that.
On the other hand, there are serious concerns of parliamentary privilege and the effects of broadcasting on parliamentary institutions.
There are many strong arguments in favour of the broadcasting of committee proceedings. A great deal of important work is done by members in committees and the public should have an opportunity to see this-The broadcasting of the proceedings of committees would provide a more balanced view of the parliamentary process and would enhance the public's perception and appreciation of the work of Parliament and parliamentarians.
The risk is that the collegiality of committees could be destroyed and replaced by a more partisan and adversarial approach by all parties.
That is something we do not want to happen.
The public has a right to know what is going on in Parliament but it is important to remember that it is a legislative body rather than a television program.
The committee's task was to establish guidelines for broadcasting that would preserve the collegial and informal atmosphere of committee meetings, thus providing a more balanced view of the parliamentary process.
We studied a couple of reports that have been very important and very instrumental in bringing this final report together. Watching the House at Work, the Cook report, provided a lot of background information and impetus to this report.
The other one was The Role and Importance of Committees, the 1985 report of the McGrath committee because that certainly changed the role of committees. It changed the importance of committees in my view. We have taken those two reports, combined them with the views, the information we heard from many, many witnesses.
Of particular importance was the information we received in the provincial legislatures of Ontario and Quebec. They took us through their process and helped us with it. We understood it and certainly, it allowed us to make decisions. In some cases it changed our views and opinions of the particular process.
It was necessary to distinguish two aspects of broadcasting. First, there is recording whereby we have gavel to gavel coverage of the committee meeting. Second, there is reporting, that is, allowing the electronic media access to committee meetings to coverage of the proceedings for recording purposes.
The committee, in its wisdom, decided upon a phasing-in approach to broadcasting, first to allow the media to record the sound or audio feed of all public committee meetings. The technology for this is already in place. This can be used by print and radio journalists very easily and television journalists could use it together with a picture of the person speaking.
We would also like to see the audio of all committee proceedings broadcast, either through OASIS or by closed-circuit FM radio. This would enable members and their staff and the media to monitor committee meetings.
Two problems presented themselves with the next phase of broadcasting. We wanted to make sure that the House was going to have the responsibility of recording and distributing tape proceedings, but those costs would be astronomical. In addition, there are just too many committee meetings to have all of them broadcast on the parliamentary channel.
The committee recommends one committee room would be set up on a non-permanent basis using existing or rented equipment at a minimum cost. The proceedings would be recorded gavel to gavel and broadcast live on OASIS and on a delayed basis on the parliamentary channel.
March 27, 1992

The recording of proceedings would be undertaken by or on behalf of the House and under direct control and supervision of the House personnel.
Given the multitude of committee meetings per day, a decision-making process must be put in place to determine which committee will be broadcast. We believe the decision should be made by the House leaders and if the House leaders are unable to agree the matter could be referred to the management committee.
We expect that a system will be devised whereby the committees and their chairmen will indicate their desire to have particular proceedings broadcast. The House leaders, of course, would take that into account, as well as public interest and fairness and reflecting the views of the different members.
We believe the issue of broadcasting committees will need to be reviewed after six months, as well as having a system set up to review complaints.
That is the essence of the report. I would just like to make one final comment if I may, and that is concerning the co-operation of the members on the committee. I want to particularly comment to the members from Saint-Leonard, Kingston and the Islands and particularly the member from Saint-Denis, who is here but is not listening to me at the present time.

Tonight in the House of Commons we are debating it. Tomorrow morning, we start again at 9.30 a.m. This is in addition to other matters.
What we are discussing of course is the subject matter of Bill C-43, the government's legislation which substantially addresses the points raised in the motion before us tonight from the member for Nickel Belt. I believe that the public trust rests on a belief and on a conviction that those in public office will conduct themselves in an ethical fashion.
Those of us holding public office, whether with great or modest responsibilities, carry with us a portion of the responsibility for the destiny of our country and for the carriage of the government of the day and also a part of the trust which the Canadian people vest in government. That is why the issue before us tonight of ethical conduct in government is one of transcending importance because in a democracy, ultimately our system of government depends upon the consent of the governed, not the coercion of the governed.
April 1, 1992

We must always see that the people of our country have confidence in those of us who are in this place and all of us, including those who are members of the Public Service, must carry out our duties in accordance with the public interest.
The issue, I would submit, is not whether a conflict of interest arises. Show me an individual who never has a conflict of interest and I will show you a one-dimensional person perhaps living in the outskirts of Frobisher Bay as a hermit. In our complex society it is inevitable that we have conflicts of interest.
The issue is not that they arise, but that when conflicts do arise, they be resolved in the public interest. That is what this bill is all about. That is what our committee is discussing; the mechanisms, the procedures, the rules that can permit all of us in public office to see that there is a way of resolving conflicts.
There are different ways that that can happen. It is by no means sufficient for those persons who hold public office in Canada to act within the law. There is a further obligation to act in a manner that will bear the closest public scrutiny.
On this point I join with the member for Nickel Belt in favouring full public disclosure. I want that to be a fundamental principle of any legislation that we enact, and then to the extent necessary to find balance and to protect the rights of privacy to which the member for York South-Weston has referred.
There can be reasonable and proper exceptions and limits, just in the same way that we have passed the Freedom of Information Act which states as a fundamental principle that all Canadians have a right to information about the public programs of our country. We make some reasonable exceptions for matters that pertain to national security, matters that pertain to sensitive commercial transactions currently under way, matters that pertain to rights of privacy of individuals and so forth, just as we do with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
We have established fundamental rights of Canadian citizens and then make some restrictions and limitations according to what can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. That is the approach that I hope we can see the legislation proceed on.

Michael Starr, both former cabinet ministers, both long-time members of this House. I believe that this report stands us in very good stead.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words at the report stage of BUI C-31, the extradition bUl. I hope to have the opportunity as well tomorrow when this comes up for third reading stage.
There are quite a few defects at the present time. Whatever else we can say about the extradition law in this country, I think we can say three things for sure. We can say that the law is enormously complex as it stands now. It results in long delays, and it requires a great deal of costly court time. It has those three defects, all of which I think most Canadians would agree should be remedied.
I suggest that the extradition bill that is presently before Parliament goes to those three problems that I find. The present legislation as it now stands gives an opportunity for an individual who is fighting extradition to get as many as three times in sequence the opportunity to have his or her case reviewed by the Supreme Court of Canada; three times in sequence.
Tell me what other forum or what other law in Canada would provide that kind of opportunity for an individual. One of the problems, and perhaps the major problem with the extradition law in this country as it is now, is that it provides that individual who has come here far more remedies than are available to a person charged with a criminal offence under Canadian law. You get far more remedies, far more kicks at the can if you have come from elsewhere to Canada to try to pursue your rights than if you are a Canadian citizen charged with an offence in this country.
As I say, you cannot give me another case where you or anyone would have a case, a problem or a charge that could be reviewed three times in sequence by the Supreme Court of Canada. You cannot come up with any examples because it only exists in the extradition law.
That is why the government, rightly so, has come forward with the changes. With respect to the motion presented by the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, I would suggest that the effect of the amendment would be to prevent the surrender of a fugitive to a foreign state until either the expiration of 30 days after the Minister of Justice makes a surrender order under section 25 or the expiration of any appeal periods or any
Government Orders
periods in which to make an application for leave to appeal, whichever time is later.
Presumably the reason for the suggested amendment is to prohibit the surrender until after the relevant appeal periods have expired in their entirety, whether or not the fugitive has actually filed an appeal or an application for leave to appeal.
The amendments contained in Bill C-31, include a statutory bar to surrender where an appeal is actually pending. In other words, a fugitive could not be surrendered where a notice of appeal has been filed on behalf of that fugitive according to the provisions of Bill C-31. These provisions do not contain a prohibition on surrender during the periods in which an appeal or leave to appeal may be initiated, if an appeal has not actually been taken.
The reason that a prohibition on surrender of the nature contemplated by the hon. member's amendment is not included in Bill C-31 is that it increases, in our opinion, the likelihood of delay. Bill C-31, on the other hand, encourages appeals on behalf of the fugitive to be initiated promptly. This is consistent with the general aim of the bill which I indicated earlier, which is to reduce delays in the handling of extradition cases in this country.
A legislative prohibition on surrender within the statutory appeal periods, where no appeal has been filed as proposed by the hon. member, has the potential to be abused by fugitives who are seeking a means to stall a likely surrender.
For example, in the case of an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, this amendment could result in a delay of up to four months before an appeal is filed where the summer recess of the court is calculated as part of the period within which to apply for leave to appeal. Otherwise the amount of time permitted to appeal to the Supreme Court under the Supreme Court of Canada Act is 60 days.
Out of concern over opening up the possibility of inordinate delay, the government is unable to support the amendment of the hon. member for Port Moody- Coquitlam. Instead the government intends to re-examine the issue of forestalling surrender of a fugitive during appeal periods.

As members have previously said, there are provinces that are currently suffering from economic shortfalls. Saskatchewan suffers from its dependency primarily on the grain trade, a trade that has been subject to the international grain price wars. Again, this is in a province that to a major degree depends on a singular aspect of its economy for its survival. There have been some attempts made to diversify, but those are somewhat limited.

There has been some comment made, yes an admission, that grants to provinces have increased over the past, but perhaps these increases have not been enough.
I am not too sure that anyone has the power, the strength, or the wherewithal to determine when enough is enough, particularly when you are reliant on a pool of funds that is restrictive in its own, and the federal government is no stranger to that dilemma.
The federal government has, and I would like to recite for you for the record, committed itself to an ever-increasing expenditure of transfer payments going to the provinces.
The EPF fund, which in 1984-85 was $14.5 billion, rose to $20.5 billion in the year 1991-92, and will go to $20,766 billion in 1992-93. In the area of equalization the same holds true going from 1984-85 from $5.5 billion up to the next year of $8.5 billion. The Canada Assistance Plan is going from $4 billion in 1984-85 to $7 billion in 1992-93 and other transfers are going from 1984-85 from $2.1 billion up to $3.6 billion in fiscal year 1992-93.
Perhaps expressed in terms of percentages, percentage figures seem to live with people more so than terms of actual dollars. EPF has increased by 4.5 per cent from 1984-85 to the year 1992-93, the equalization funds by 5.9 per cent and the Canada Assistance Plan by 7.3 per cent.
It is very clear that there have been ongoing increases in the transfer payments from the federal government to the provinces. What makes this point even much more important to make is that all of this has occurred at a time when the federal government has dug in and said: "We will reduce our expenditures at a time when others are asking us to increase our expenditures". Canadians generally are asking the Government of Canada to reduce its expenditures and in so doing we have had to limit the rate of growth that has been transferred to other provinces.
I made issue of this just last week in a Standing Order 31 statement where we have been criticized for what is more popularly referred to as off-loading. To curtail the rate of growth, to still include a rate of growth in the
Government Orders
amount of funds going to the provinces, I would suggest respectfully that it is not off-loading.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, on September 17, 1991 the Minister of Justice tabled in the House of Commons Bill C-31, which is the culmination of efforts to reduce the inordinate delays that are currently possible in extradition cases.
The need for the amendments contained in this bill, I would suggest, is urgent. Canadians are deeply concerned about the legal system operating as an impediment to Canada being able to return persons wanted for trial or sentence to foreign jurisdictions.

April 7, 1992
Government Orders
One source of the excessive delays is the dual tracks available for the appeals of extradition decisions. The extradition process has two stages: the judicial stage where a judge decides whether there is sufficient evidence against the person requested by the foreign state to subject him or her to surrender, and the executive stage where the Minister of Justice has to decide whether to surrender the requested person.
Currently in an extradition case, an appeal of the decision of the extradition judge and a review of the decision of the Minister of Justice are held consecutively. A decision of the extradition judge is subject to basic court proceedings.
An appeal of the decision can then be heard by the provincial or territorial courts of appeal and eventually by the Supreme Court of Canada. It is only after appeals, if any, have been exhausted that the Minister of Justice is requested to surrender the fugitive. A decision of the Minister of Justice can be reviewed by the Federal Court and then by the Supreme Court of Canada.
The provisions of the bill detail the means available to challenge the judicial and ministerial decisions which are made after Canada receives an extradition request from a foreign state.
Bill C-31 also presents a means to avoid the use of these two lengthy tracks which are now available to challenge decisions in extradition cases and delay surrender. In particular, the bill provides a right of appeal of decisions rendered by the extradition judge to the provincial or territorial courts of appeal on specific grounds.
It also provides the same courts with the power to review decisions of the Minister of Justice. In other words, the same courts will hear appeals and review decisions of the minister. It thereby creates a general ability to deal with these issues in place at one time.
Therefore, in most cases appeal and review procedures will be combined into the provincial or territorial courts of appeal. That level of court will have a comprehensive power to control the appeal and review processes, as well as examine both judicial and ministerial decisions and ensure that appeals and reviews are conducted efficiently and early.
To further reduce delay, time limits within various steps in the extradition process are stipulated in the bill.
First the fugitive generally has 30 days after a judge finds there is sufficient evidence to order surrender within which to make submissions to the Minister of Justice. Only where it is appropriate may the minister receive submissions after the 30-day time period.
The requesting person or requesting state has 30 days after the judge's decision to file a notice of appeal regarding the court's decision. Subject to limited exceptions, the Minister of Justice is required to decide on surrender within 90 days of the decision by a judge that there is sufficient evidence to extradite the fugitive.
The bill provides recourse if the decision on surrender is not made within the stipulated time period. The fugitive can apply to be released if the Minister of Justice does not show cause why a decision about surrender was not made within the 90-day time period.
As well, if the fugitive has not been removed from Canada within a period of 45 days from the time the surrender order has been made by the Minister of Justice or after the appeals from such an order has been taken, he or she may make an application for release. These clear-cut and time specific procedures will expedite extradition cases.
Additionally, proceedings will be streamlined by the ability of the judge in an extradition case to hear arguments based on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms instead of the current situation whereby the judge hears such arguments. This particular amendment permits all legal matters related to the extradition hearing to be dealt with by the judge at one time.
While the effects of the amendment are basically to speed up the extradition process, it does not remove appropriate protections for the person sought. Alleged charter violations will be dealt with and appeals and review are provided of the decisions made by the judge and the minister.
Therefore, in addition to expediting the extradition process, the bill ensures that the person sought is afforded appropriate protections. Injecting greater efficiency into our extradition process will not occur at the expense of the rights of the person sought. I believe the bill strikes the proper balance between the clear need for efficiency in extradition cases and the importance of safeguarding the rights of individuals.

Canadians are disheartened and Canadians lack any hope, not only in this national government but as a result of the report card and the litany of experiences they have had to endure and survive for the last eight years. to be indifferent and cynical toward governments, politicians and national institutions.
When our House leader this morning put before this Chamber a motion of non-confidence, it was done, not for any jockeying back and forth in this House, but it was done on behalf of the mood of some 26 million Canadians from coast to coast to coast. There are by any account, by any poll, roughly 85 per cent of Canadians who neither like nor want this national government. That means that only 15 per cent-and I cannot find them anywhere-still have some confidence in the leadership of this national government.
We think those numbers are alarming, or they should be alarming to the members on the other side, because how are they to lead and inspire a country when, out of 100 people, 85 people do not wish to follow them and, moreover, have said in a number of polls, never again.
I am not suggesting that every poll is right or that every election from here on in is a foregone conclusion. I am not. What I am saying and what we are saying in the motion is that we have a country that is psychologically tired of the direction and leadership being offered by this government.

They do want an election as a way of opening the windows and allowing in some fresh air, some new air to this home called Canada. I am not saying that we are perfect, that we have all the answers or that we will indeed be the alternative. That is to be earned.
We will certainly do our share and work to demonstrate that we are capable, ready and able to capture that if in fact Canadians wish to bestow that authority on us. What we are saying and what Canadians are certainly reflecting is the desire to allow Canadians to decide.
After all, as the fall approaches we will be in the fourth year of this mandate. This Prime Minister in his pre-life as Prime Minister always said that governments should not go any longer than four years. Four years has been a well-deserved tradition in this country. He has said that under no circumstances should a government go beyond four years.
Now we have the same Prime Minister suggesting to Canadians that they should put out of their mind any
election before 1993, the fifth year of this government's mandate. How handy it has been for this Prime Minister now to argue intellectually things that were repugnant to him only a few years ago.
Yet the message that Canadians are sending to this government is that this government is not there for the Prime Minister to tinker with. This is not his country to experiment with, FTA one year and NAFTA another and perhaps play with the different regions, because this country is here for the long term.
This government is only given a temporary mandate. The decisions that we have been seeing since 1984 have been decisions that have gone to the very root of this country. In the opinion of the majority, those, decisions are certainly not in the best interests of this country.
We have Canadians who want the ability to decide and choose a new government. We have Canadians who, economically speaking, are hurting in every region of the country.

You could not go into a cafe. You could not have a constituency appointment. You could not go to a social function on a Friday or Saturday evening without being consumed in discussion after discussion with average Torontonians on the situation of the economy.
I was running into people who for the first time were unemployed and felt undignified in asking how to fill out a UI application. When you ask Canadians: Do you have economic renewal? Does the FTA help you in Toronto? Do the 400,000 jobs that we lost in manufacturing alone bode for a better future? On the Constitution, where this government promised national reconciliation, we have a divided House like never before.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the comments on this bill, but the hon. member knows the federal government already provides substantial assistance to students attending institutions for post-secondary education. This assistance is threefold. First, the federal government transfers substantial amounts to the provinces and territories every year. About $6 billion is transferred annually through EPF programs for post-secondary education.
The provinces and territories may use these funds as they see fit. Furthermore, about $8 billion is transferred annually to the poorer provinces in the form of equalization payments. There are no strings attached, so that the provinces are free to spend these funds on education or on other services for which they are responsible.
April 28, 1992

Private Members' Business
Second, the federal government provides assistance under the Canada Student Loans Program, to help students from low income families attend institutions for post-secondary education. The program provides for loans totalling approximately $635 million for about
215.000	students annually. Until the students have finished their studies, the interest on these loans is paid by the federal government.
Third, the federal Income Tax Act contains a number of measures that provide tax relief for students. A tax credit is available for tuition fees paid to post-secondary institutions.
About 1.1 million students claimed this credit for the 1992 fiscal year, thus reducing their federal income tax by $130 million. Students may also claim an education tax credit based on the number of months of full-time study at a post-secondary institution.
For the 1992 fiscal year, this credit was claimed by
585.000	students who were able to reduce their federal income tax by $35 million. When students are unable to use all their tuition fee and education credits, the unused portion may be transferred to their spouse, a parent or grandparent, up to a certain maximum. About 400,000 spouses, parents and grandparents were able to reduce their income tax by $20 million in 1992.
Finally, the federal tax system also allows an exemption of $500 of bursary income. This measure provides tax relief for over 160,000 students, totalling $20 million.
In the 1992 budget we announced that the dollar limit on which the education credit is calculated would be increased by one-third, to $80 per month of full-time study. In addition, the limit on the total amount of tuition fee and education credits that may be claimed by another taxpayer will be increased from $600 to $680. These changes will benefit 600,000 students claiming the education tax credit and 400,000 taxpayers claiming the transfer. These changes will reduce federal tax revenues by about $25 million annually.
Finally, education is largely a provincial responsibility. Generally speaking, there are no tuition or registration fees for primary and secondary education. Since post-secondary education is partly financed by tuition fees, the federal government has traditionally provided direct and indirect assistance to students at the post-secondary level.
That was more or less what I had to say. Although the hon. member made some very good points, I believe that since education is a provincial responsibility, it would be appropriate for the provinces to implement this proposal.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to debate further the issues contained in Bill C-71, an act to amend the Criminal Records Act and other acts in consequence thereof.

May 5, 1992
Government Orders
I want to say right off the bat that my colleagues on this side of the House and I accept as good and prudent the matters that are contained in the bill.
The bill addresses a problem that had developed over the years and was made apparent by interventions of a number of members of the House of Commons. My only minor criticism is that it took so long to effect such a minor change.
Having said that, there was another issue which became apparent to many of us in this House. That was the delay that was developing in the granting of pardons under the Criminal Records Act.
There were many people who were prima facie entitled to the pardons. They deserved them under the terms of the legislation, but it was taking a long time, in many cases upwards or in excess of one year to deal with the pardon, thereby preventing the applicant from getting on with aspects of his or her life that would have required the pardon. This bill attempts to deal with that.
This area of criminal records and the amendments here, the approach taken by the government, is a little bit like putting a foot into a worn-out shoe and patching it. I have had an opportunity to read this bill several times since being elected three years ago.
I am of the view that the bill is extremely weak. I think that the bill had its roots in a previous Liberal government, but this bill does not do the job. It is extremely weak. I want to point that out for the record. Hopefully the committee that takes this bill will be able to address some of these problems. I know the Solicitor General has been listening of late. Not quite a death bed repentance but the new Solicitor General has been listening to the justice committee and listening to Canadians. I do not want to give too much credit, sitting in opposition here, but I certainly want to give credit where credit is due.
The bill does, in band-aid fashion, address the problem of conditional discharges where individuals who were discharged at trial following conviction, either absolutely or conditionally, were still required under the existing legislation to go back and get a pardon for an offence which the Criminal Code says was deemed never to have been committed. That is a little bit like catch-22
in 1984. This bill does address that. Now those who have been discharged subject to a waiting period which will expire automatically will not have a criminal record, as was originally intended by the discharge sections of the Criminal Code. Well, good for them.
The other thing it will do is it will revoke automatically a pardon which was given under the statute where the individual involved subsequently commits an indictable offence. If you have been a good guy, good for you; if you commit an indictable offence after a pardon has been given, back to square one, your conviction is reinstated. That is quite fair and appropriate.
On a procedural basis, the National Parole Board has been given jurisdiction and authority to administer and grant the pardons. That will obviate the need to send all of those pieces of paper to cabinet to get the signatures of ministers and all of the procedure that is involved in there. That is appropriate. It is a good fit.
However, here is what is missing. I want to start with the title of this bill because the title does not even fit. The name of the bill is the Criminal Records Act. I want to say that the bill does not deal with the management of criminal records. It never did. It never had the intention to.
It is a bill to get rid of the criminal record, to use layman's parlance. That is what the bill is for. It should have been called the pardons act or the pardon of a criminal act or a record of conviction, something along those lines. The title was not a fit from that perspective.
There is another problem. As I stand here, I do not understand why the bill-keep in mind, we are dealing with what the bill calls criminal records-does not define what a criminal record is. That is of absolutely no help to those who administer the act. In fact, it is a hindrance and, as I hope to point out, a serious fatal flaw in achieving under the bill what I think everyone wanted to achieve many years ago. The bill does not contain a definition.
In addition to not having a definition of what a criminal record is, a bill dealing with criminal records, the bill also deals with pardons. What else does the bill not have? It does not have a definition of what a pardon is.

Motion 538 is being debated just as the external review of the Canadian drug approval system or process is scheduled for completion in June. Therefore this debate is very timely. Private Members' Business
The House should be aware that the review is really being prompted by cuts in budget to Health and Welfare. Let us look at the budget for the Health Protection Branch in the last three years. In 1990-91 it was $65.6 million and had 734 person-years. This year it has been reduced to $64.4 million and 715 person-years, a reduction of 19 person-years. In effect, the branch has gone backwards with regard to funding and personnel for dealing with drug approvals for the past three years. No wonder such antagonists as the generic drug manufacturers and the brand name manufacturers agree that a quicker method for approval must be found.
There is little doubt that Professor Gagnon is expected to arrive at the obviously preferred solution of privatization. Even if he does not, the present fiscal climate will dictate it. Indeed outside persons are playing a role already in drug approval and it certainly will be expanded by this government.
Before we privatize the testing system, should we not be aware of the risks? In making inquiries about the testing of pharmaceuticals I have learned there is a simple equation. If clinical tests of drug effectiveness are performed in faster time, less data will result. That means if tests are conducted with hundreds of humans, the effects that occur in one in one thousand will not be detected and there are going to be difficulties.
Perhaps the best known case is thalidomide. Thalidomide was a typical modem minor therapeutic drug produced by major drug manufacturers, which was approved in some countries but not in others. Once these tragedies occur they are irreversible. Given the differences in liability law, it has meant a very unequal life for the children who have been affected.
There are other much more recent cases where we have had controversial drags. In the last few months concerns about Prozac and Halcion have been raised. We have also had medical devices with continued problems, such as the Meme breast implant. These situations still exist. The question is whether we want more or less of
them. The answer is that we will get more if we privatize the approval process.
There are other risks in the privatized system. In Canada we have seen the scandals of testing done in the 1980s by Industrial Bio-Test, a U.S. firm. In seeking approval for products it had been commissioned to test, IBT simply falsified test results. These tests were for agricultural chemicals and Agriculture Canada had to spend much valuable time and effort to confirm whether the material it received was true.

Each additional month of marketing time means millions in sales, given the kind of high-priced drug promotion that goes on in Canada today. Without professionally disinterested public servants being central to the process, the pressure for cheating could be enormous, particularly when a rival drug in a similar stage is seeking approval.

The U.S. government and U.S. multinationals have unilaterally forced us to change our generic drug laws. It is what the multinational drug companies want, and that is what we will get from this government.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have been awakened by events of the past week in Los Angeles and yesterday in Toronto. I am sure
people right across this country have a new sense of awareness about how much racism is a part of our lives.
We have been awakened to the tragedy of violent riots precipitated by feelings of racism which, undoubtedly, were an expression of the frustration and anger of young people, in particular, who have little hope.
Violence such as we saw in Toronto must not be condoned. As many speakers have said, we must support actions to deal with it. It must be seen by all of us as a symptom of deeper ills, of poverty, of lack of education and of unemployment. It certainly reflects the frustration of young people of colour, in particular, who feel they are in a society where systemic discrimination and racism are a fact of life and that they have little or no opportunity for the future.
It happened in Toronto and Los Angeles but let us not kid ourselves in other parts of Canada. It could also happen in our communities.
It started in Toronto with the shooting of a black man by police who possibly had no alternative. There have been too many examples of shootings of blacks in Toronto and a great racism against black citizens in Halifax.
Our justice system has a double standard for aboriginals and people of colour. The government must act now to stop racism. Minorities are frustrated and angered by the inequalities they see and experience in their daily lives. We must not tolerate criminal responses but we must understand the causes of the anger and violence that we saw expressed yesterday and last week.
We must deal with unemployment and poverty and not just talk about statistics. We must deal with economic and social programs that will open opportunities for young people and, in particular, create jobs.
We must feed hungry children in inner city schools but their parents must have opportunities to work with pride, dignity and respect.
As Canadians we must not be complacent. We take too much pride in thinking that we are very accepting and that we do not discriminate. We should be outraged at events in our history, past and present, that discriminated against our neighbours and against fellow citizens across Canada.

The Manitoba Native Justice Commission documented deeply embedded and institutionalized racism against aboriginal persons as did the Donald Marshall
case in Nova Scotia.
In my province of British Columbia, we have a history of overt racism starting with the Komagata Mam incident, the denial of the right to vote for Asians and the discriminatory, racist Chinese head tax and exclusion act. Japanese Canadian citizens were interned in my riding at the PNE grounds.
Now we have neo-Nazis and skinheads preaching hate, burning crosses and operating hate hot lines. Of course, these are a few people who are instigating such racist activities. In the past it was racist legislation but citizens no longer will tolerate that on the whole. We cannot be complacent and we cannot say that we are an accepting, non-racist society that treats all people equally and with respect.
Let us hope that yesterday's events, like last year's tragic events at Oka, will bring a new public awareness that racism is a sickness that can and must be stamped out.
I call on parliamentarians on all sides of the House to work together to support a proactive plan of action to eliminate racism. We must all support the government in acting now to implement a plan of action which could include the following eight points.

We must strengthen the Canadian Human Rights Commission to effectively deal with complaints and systemic discrimination and racism. They must have more resources to do this.
We must proclaim Bill C-63 which we passed in the last House and establish the Canadian Race Relations Foundation with a strong mandate to eliminate racism. We need realistic targets to employ visible minority staff based on availability rates.
Finally, we must immediately acknowledge the past racism in our Canadian history. I think we should do this, first of all, by redressing the racist Chinese head tax and exclusion act which discriminated against people because of their race. We must learn from the past.
I appeal to the government, to the minister and to other members of the House to take a proactive position now. Let us not wait for the next election. Canadians who believe in justice and fairness demand concrete action by their members of Parliament and by their government.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with all those who have spoken thus far on these particular amendments, and say that it is absolutely critical that Parliament reassert itself in this area and carry out that part of its function.

My colleague referred to the paper submitted by Professor Stuart Farson to our committee. I would like to read a portion of it because it summarizes exactly where we are and what we are trying to do:
In my view, on each and every occasion when Parliament hands over or delegates a responsibility to another body, such an action has the potential both for detracting from Parliament's sovereignty, and for limiting democracy by increasing the power of the executive and the bureaucracy. Care must, therefore, be taken to ensure that there are off-setting factors in play. If Parliament is to fulfil its public-interest role, it must be able to assure itself-as a minimum-that those to whom it has delegated the investigatory or review functions on its behalf actually do ask the questions that Parliament would want to ask; and do obtain full answers to them in a timely fashion. Particular attention, therefore, has to be paid to what investigatory bodies may see, and how they can, and do, communicate with Parliament. This will mean that investigatory or review bodies should be an open book to Parliament, albeit, if necessary, through an all-party committee meeting in camera.

Government Orders

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I too am very pleased today to rise and say a few words in support of Bill C-227.
As our country's symbol, the value of the Canadian flag cannot be measured. Our flag is based on the traditions and values upon which this country was founded. It represents more than nationhood and patriotism. It also represents the very character of Canada which makes this country the most unique and greatest country in the world.
It has been said that a flag speaks for the people of a nation. The flag is used in celebration when it is raised at holidays and at other festivities. It also expresses our sorrow when flown at half-mast. The flag also expresses our reverence for those who have given their lives in its name in wartime or while in keeping the peace.
The purpose of this bill is to instil the necessity of respecting the importance of the flag's past role and its continuing symbol of what Canada is today by providing that anyone who wilfully burns, defaces, defiles, mutilates, tramples upon or otherwise desecrates the Canadian flag will be guilty of a criminal offence. This bill will ensure the protection of and respect for the ideals upon which this great country has been founded.

Private Members' Business
The idea of the Canadian flag was born back in March 1964, during a chance meeting between a former eastern Ontario member of Parliament and United Empire Loyalist, Mr. John Matheson and George Stanley, a one-time Dean of Arts at the Royal Military College in Kingston, Ontario.
At the time the government was considering the possibility of providing Canada with a distinctive Canadian flag. When informed of this intention by Mr. Matheson, Mr. Stanley drew a design of a maple leaf on a red and white background. He later submitted a memorandum to the government listing the traditional symbols of Canada. The beaver and the maple leaf were on the top of that list.
In early 1964 the Prime Minister of the day had informed the House that the government had a desire to adopt a truly distinctive national flag. The ensuing debate about the design of the flag has been described many times as no less fierce. It demonstrates the intense devotion Canadians from across the country feel about Canada.
The official ceremony inaugurating the new Canadian flag which was held on February 15, 1965 was a very emotional time. On that day the Speaker of the Senate at the time said that the flag was a symbol of the nation's unity for it, beyond any doubt, represents all the citizens of Canada without distinction of race, language, belief or opinion. These words add further symbolic meaning to our flag and illustrate that our flag is more than just mere identification. It is representative of the very character, substance and spirit of this great nation.
In realizing the importance of the Canadian flag, what it really represents or stands for and the emotion it evokes among Canadians, it should be our duty to make sure that it is properly protected.
There are those who have said, especially our neighbours to the south where similar legislation has twice been ruled unconstitutional by the United States Supreme Court, that laws such as the one proposed in this particular bill infringe upon society's right to freedom of speech. I certainly disagree with these arguments. Protection of the flag, a unique symbol of nationality, will in no way limit the opportunity or the breadth of protest available in the exercise of freedom of speech. Freedom of speech must not extend to
those who would damage another national symbol, the Parliament Buildings for example.
I seek only to protect the national symbol which is just as, and maybe more significant, our Canadian flag. Protecting our flag will not inhibit other forms of protest such as speech, the use of placards or literature or any other number of peaceful, non-violent actions. It simply will ensure the protection of the unique symbol which Canadians, time and time again, have shown to be the one thing which most represents Canada and what it is about: the best place in the world to live.
This year, 1992, as we know marks Canada's 125th anniversary. Our history stretches back to the First Nations of this land. It embraces such beliefs as those of the United Empire Loyalists many of whom settled in eastern Ontario, who over two centuries ago sought a better life. And it spreads out to include people from all nations of the world who arrived here looking for freedom and prosperity.
Our flag has come to embody this heritage, our pride in our country today and our hopes for the future. I think it is more than fitting that we preserve and ensure respect for our national symbol.
For that reason, I certainly want to add my congratulations to the member for Scarborough East for his introduction of this bill. I am very pleased to offer support on behalf of the proud Canadians I represent in Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington, a historic part Canada, settled by United Empire Loyalists over 200 years ago and the home of Canada's first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, an architect of Confederation.
Our flag is the greatest symbol of national unity.

I would hope that the parliamentary secretary who will be responding to my concerns and to the questions I have raised will reconsider the approach of the Government of Canada and put pressure, real pressure, on other foreign nations that are doing overfishing in our waters and outside our 200-mile limit.

BasePK: 3909572

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on second reading of Bill C-81, an act that will enable the Government of Canada to consult Canadians by means of a referendum.
Basically, the purpose of this bill is to provide Canadians with a fair and democratic instrument to settle the constitutional debate, once and for all.
I think it is important to point out that there has been no decision by the government to hold a referendum on the constitutional question. It is by no means certain that this type of consultation will take place. In fact, we on this side of the House would prefer not to have to hold a referendum.
The government has said repeatedly that its primary objective is to reach a firm constitutional agreement through the discussions currently taking place with our provincial, territorial and aboriginal partners. Considering what has been accomplished in the past few months, we can be reasonably optimistic about the outcome of the current process.
In any event, we intend to focus all our efforts on reaching a political and negotiated solution to our constitutional problems. However, we must be ready for any eventuality. The bill before the House today should be seen as a precautionary measure and as an insurance policy for all Canadians.
Basically, this bill is a democratic extension of the current consultation process. From the outset, Canadians have made it clear that they did not want to be left out of the constitutional process. That is why our initiatives in this area have included a high degree of consultation, and we can be justly proud of the results.
First of all, the Citizens' Forum on the Future of Canada went to communities throughout the country and listened to thousands of Canadians. Cabinet ministers met many Canadians to find out what they had to say

May 19, 1992
Government Orders
about the future of their country. Subsequently, the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee examined various aspects of the amending formula. Finally, between last fall and the end of February, the Special Joint Committee on a Renewed Canada went to all the provinces and territories, received more than 3,000 briefs and held 78 sittings for a total of 227 hours, during which it heard 700 witnesses.
The government's purpose in tabling this bill is also to ensure that the rules of the game for any consultation that takes place will be fair, open and transparent, in accordance with our democratic traditions and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
What are those rules, Mr. Speaker? Basically, they would be the same as for a general election. The referendum would be supervised by the Chief Electoral Officer and be subject to the provisions of the Canada Elections Act, already a guarantee of a fair process. Furthermore, the "yes" and "no" sides would have equal access to free air time, as determined by the arbitrator. The CRTC would also supervise the purchase of air time on radio and television networks for advertising purposes.
However, there are some differences because of the very nature of this kind of consultation and the implications of the charter. First of all, the bill does not make so-called umbrella committees mandatory. Any obligation to take part in the referendum campaign under the aegis of such committees would be contrary to the Charter of Rights, according to the legal opinions we have received so far. In fact, such an obligation would not only be likely to violate freedom of expression, it would also force groups that may be for or against the question for entirely different reasons to operate under the same umbrella.
What should be understood is that the situation is entirely different from the referendum held in Quebec in 1980. At the time, both options were represented by a political party which headed an umbrella committee. That would not be the case in a Canadian referendum on constitutional reform. In this connection I would like to quote the senior editor of La Presse, Mr. Alain Dubuc, who wrote the following on May 14:
If we apply the Quebec model to the Canadian referendum, the result is frankly grotesque. This is especially true when we consider the umbrella-committee concept. Any attempt to put those who say
yes to constitutional reform in one group and those who say no in
another group makes a mockery of democracy.
However we believe Canadians have the right to know all the details of the process. That is why the bill contains some very clear provisions to ensure the referendum campaign's funding process is absolutely transparent.
